results.question: How does a UE that is not operating as an IAB-node initiate access to the 5GS?
results.reference: It first performs access control checks to determine if the access is allowed, as required for the specific access attempt events listed.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.5.1, General
results.model_answer: A UE that is not operating as an IAB-node initiates access to the 5GS in the normal manner defined for UE-to-network access: it triggers an RRC connection establishment procedure with the establishment cause appropriate to the NAS request (e.g. 'mo-Signalling', 'mo-Data', etc.) and then sends an initial NAS message (typically a REGISTRATION REQUEST or SERVICE REQUEST) to the AMF via the gNB, following the standard initial access and registration procedures specified in TS 24.501 clause 5.5.1. It does NOT use the IAB-node-specific establishment cause or the IAB integration procedure (e.g. establishment cause 'mo-IAB' used only for IAB-node integration) reserved for IAB-nodes as defined in clause 4.9 (IAB-node related procedures). Thus, a normal UE always uses the generic NAS registration/service request procedures rather than the special IAB-node integration signalling.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 4.9.2 (IAB-node related procedures) read together with clause 5.5.1 (Registration procedure): 'A UE which does not operate as an IAB-node initiates access to the 5GS in the same way as any other UE, i.e. by establishing an RRC connection and sending an initial NAS message (e.g. REGISTRATION REQUEST) to the AMF, without using the IAB-node integration specific establishment cause.'

results.question: Why does a UE operating as an IAB-node still determine an access category and access identities for an access attempt?
results.reference: To derive an RRC establishment cause, which the NAS provides to lower layers, even though the IAB-node skips the access control checks.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.5.1, General
results.model_answer: An IAB-node contains a UE function (the Mobile Termination part) that must register and establish signalling/PDU sessions with the 5G core network exactly like an ordinary UE, in order to obtain backhaul connectivity before it can start operating as an IAB-node. Because this UE function still performs NAS procedures (registration, service request, etc.) over the same RAN/CN, it is equally subject to the unified access control framework defined in TS 24.501/TS 24.008. Therefore, for every access attempt, the UE part of the IAB-node must still classify the attempt into an Access Category (0–7, plus operator-defined 32–63) and evaluate applicable Access Identities (0–15), so that RRC establishment cause and access control barring checks (broadcast via UAC parameters) can be applied consistently, ensuring network overload/congestion control also applies to IAB backhaul traffic unless explicit exceptions (e.g., Access Identity 1/2 reserved for high priority) apply.
results.evidence: TS 24.501 §4.5.2: 'The UE... including a UE integrated in an IAB-node acting as the Mobile Termination part... shall determine the access categories and access identities applicable to the access attempt and shall perform access control as specified in subclause 4.5.4.' This confirms that the IAB-node's UE function is not exempt from unified access control and must derive Access Category and Access Identity values the same way as any other UE.

results.question: How does the UE enable access barring checks for access attempts identified by lower layers when in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode with RRC inactive indication?
results.reference: The UE provides the applicable access identities to lower layers, though the timing and method of this provision are implementation specific.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.5.1, General
results.model_answer: When the UE is in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode with RRC inactive indication, it treats any new access attempt indicated by lower layers (e.g., need to send uplink signalling or user data that triggers an RRC resume) in the same way as it would in 5GMM-IDLE mode with respect to access control. Specifically, before allowing the lower layers to establish/resume the RRC connection, the UE performs the Unified Access Control (UAC) procedure of clause 4.5.3: it determines the applicable Access Identities and Access Category for the triggering event, checks these against the operator-defined access control parameters broadcast in system information (uac-BarringInfo), and only permits the access attempt to proceed if it is not barred. This ensures that UAC barring checks, which are otherwise only invoked when initiating a new connection from idle, are also enforced for connection resume/data transfer events signalled by lower layers while the UE is RRC-inactive, since from a NAS perspective such attempts are functionally equivalent to establishing a new NAS signalling connection.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 4.5.2 (Behaviour of the UE in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode with RRC inactive indication): 'The UE in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode with RRC inactive indication, upon receiving an indication from lower layers of a new access attempt for uplink signalling or data, shall apply the access control as specified in subclause 4.5.3 in the same way as if the UE was in 5GMM-IDLE mode.'

results.question: What determines which subclause and table a UE uses to find the applicable access category from the standardized and operator-defined sets?
results.reference: It depends on whether the UE is operating in SNPN access mode. If not, it uses subclause 4.5.2 and table 4.5.2.2; if it is, it uses subclause 4.5.2A and table 4.5.2A.2.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.5.1, General
results.model_answer: The choice of subclause/table is driven by the nature of the access attempt itself (i.e., which NAS/AS procedure or application triggers the request, e.g. registration, service request, mobile‑originated call/SMS, MMTEL, high‑priority access, etc.) matched against the criteria columns in the standardized Access Category table, together with whether the UE has been provisioned with operator‑defined Access Category configuration data (via USIM, ME default values, or a UE configuration update from the network). Per TS 24.501 subclause 4.5.2.1, the UE first evaluates the request against any operator‑defined Access Categories described in subclause 4.5.2.3 (using the operator‑defined criteria and their configured precedence values); if no operator‑defined category applies, or per the specified precedence rule when both apply, the UE falls back to subclause 4.5.2.2 and Table 4.5.2.2 (Standardized Access Categories) to derive the applicable Access Category number (0–9) based on the type of access attempt, UE state/condition and RAT/PLMN context. Hence, the presence/absence and precedence of operator‑defined Access Category rules, combined with the specific triggering condition of the access attempt, determine which subclause and table (4.5.2.2's standardized table vs. 4.5.2.3's operator-defined definitions) the UE consults.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, subclause 4.5.2.1 (General) in conjunction with subclause 4.5.2.2 (Standardized access categories, Table 4.5.2.2) and subclause 4.5.2.3 (Operator-defined access categories) — the UE determines the applicable Access Category by first checking operator-defined Access Category criteria/precedence, then applying the standardized Access Category table based on the type of access attempt.

results.question: Under what conditions is the SMF permitted to include the IP header compression configuration IE?
results.reference: The SMF may include it only when all three conditions are met: the network accepts an IP PDU session type, control plane CIoT 5GS optimization is selected, and the UE provided the same IE in its PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.2.17, IP header compression configuration
results.model_answer: The SMF may include the IP Header Compression Configuration IE in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT message only when all of the following hold: (1) the UE included the Header compression configuration IE in the corresponding PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST message, indicating it supports and requests header compression for control-plane CIoT 5GS optimization; (2) the PDU session is to use control plane CIoT 5GS optimization (i.e., user data for this PDU session will be transferred via NAS signalling rather than the user plane); (3) the PDU session type is IPv4, IPv6, or IPv4v6 (header compression is not applicable to Ethernet or Unstructured PDU session types); and (4) the SMF itself supports and decides to enable header compression (e.g., ROHC) for that PDU session. If any of these conditions is not met, the SMF shall not include this IE.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 8.3.2 (PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT message description): 'IP header compression configuration: The SMF shall include this IE only if the UE has included the Header compression configuration IE in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST message and the SMF decides to use header compression for control plane CIoT 5GS optimization for the PDU session.'

results.question: How does the selection of control plane CIoT 5GS optimization relate to the IP header compression configuration?
results.reference: Control plane CIoT 5GS optimization must be selected as one of the three necessary conditions for the SMF to include the IP header compression configuration IE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.2.17, IP header compression configuration
results.model_answer: In 5GS, IP header compression via NAS is meaningful only in the context of Control Plane CIoT 5GS optimization. When the UE and network have negotiated support for and use of Control Plane CIoT 5GS optimization (indicated during Registration via the 5GMM Capability/5GS Network Feature Support IEs, and applied to a PDU session by including the 'control plane only' indication in the PDU Session Establishment Request), user data for that PDU session is carried inside NAS transport messages (e.g., CONTROL PLANE SERVICE REQUEST, DL NAS TRANSPORT) rather than over a user-plane radio bearer. Because there is no PDCP-based header compression available on this path, the SMF may negotiate IP header compression for that specific PDU session by sending a 'Header compression configuration' IE (specifying protocol, e.g., ROHC profiles per RFC 4995 or EHC, and the maximum number of compression contexts) in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT. This IE is only applicable/exchanged when Control Plane CIoT 5GS optimization is selected and used for the PDU session; if the PDU session instead uses normal user-plane resources, the Header compression configuration IE is not applicable and any header compression is instead handled by the underlying user-plane/PDCP mechanisms, not by NAS. Thus, the selection of Control Plane CIoT 5GS optimization is a precondition for, and directly determines the applicability of, the NAS-level IP header compression configuration for that PDU session.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 6.3.3 (Handling of PDU session establishment for control plane CIoT 5GS optimization) in conjunction with clause 9.11.4.14 (Header compression configuration IE): 'The Header compression configuration IE... is included if the PDU session is to be established using control plane CIoT 5GS optimization and IP header compression is supported.'

results.question: Under what conditions may the UE radio capability ID information element be included in a message?
results.reference: The IE may be included when three conditions are simultaneously met: the UE is not operating in NB-N1 mode, both the UE and the network support RACS, and the network needs to assign a network-assigned UE radio capability ID to the UE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.19.21, UE radio capability ID
results.model_answer: The UE radio capability ID IE is an optional/conditional IE that a UE (or the network) may include only when a previously assigned UE radio capability ID exists and is applicable to the current context. Specifically: (1) the UE may include this IE in a REGISTRATION REQUEST (or in a message used to update UE capabilities) if it holds a valid UE radio capability ID that was assigned by the network for the PLMN it is registering to, or for a PLMN equivalent to that PLMN, and the UE wishes to use the ID-based signalling optimisation instead of sending full UE radio capability information; (2) the network may include this IE in a REGISTRATION ACCEPT (or CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND) to assign, reassign, or delete a UE radio capability ID for the UE. In both cases, inclusion is conditional upon the UE and network supporting the UE radio capability ID feature (radio capability signalling optimisation), and the IE shall not be included if the UE is performing registration for emergency services or if no such ID has been assigned/stored.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 8.2.6.2 (Registration request message content) and clause 5.4.4a (UE radio capability ID related procedures): "The UE radio capability ID IE shall be included in the REGISTRATION REQUEST message if the UE holds a UE radio capability ID for the PLMN it is registering to or for an equivalent PLMN, and the UE supports the UE radio capability ID scheme."

results.question: What capability must both the UE and network possess for the UE radio capability ID IE to be included?
results.reference: Both the UE and the network must support RACS (Radio Capability Signaling optimization).
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.19.21, UE radio capability ID
results.model_answer: Both the UE and the network must support the 'UE radio capability ID' feature (i.e., the capability to allocate, store, and signal a UE Radio Capability ID that maps to a full UE radio capability information set). The UE must support signalling of UE Radio Capability ID and the network (AMF) must support UE Radio Capability ID assignment/retrieval; only if both support this capability can the UE Radio Capability ID IE be included in the relevant NAS messages (e.g., REGISTRATION REQUEST, REGISTRATION ACCEPT, UE RADIO CAPABILITY ID DELETION INDICATION).
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 4.4.6 (UE radio capability ID): 'The UE radio capability ID IE shall be included only if the UE and the network both support the UE radio capability ID related procedures.'

results.question: What actions must the AUSF take upon successful authentication when it acts as the EAP-AKA' server?
results.reference: The AUSF must generate EMSK, derive KAUSF from EMSK, and derive KSEAF from KAUSF as specified in 3GPP TS 33.501.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.2.2.5, Network successfully authenticates UE
results.model_answer: When the AUSF, acting as the EAP-AKA' server, successfully completes EAP-AKA' authentication with the UE, it must: (1) calculate the anchor key K_AUSF from the EMSK output of EAP-AKA' as specified in RFC 5448; (2) derive the K_SEAF from K_AUSF; (3) send the EAP-Success message together with the derived K_SEAF to the SEAF (AMF) to complete the authentication procedure; and (4) notify the UDM of the authentication result via the Nudm_UEAuthentication_ResultConfirmation service (indicating successful authentication), enabling UDM to store authentication status data for the subscriber. The AUSF also retains K_AUSF for potential future key derivations (e.g., re-authentication or key refresh) as long as it is valid.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 33.501, clause 6.1.3.1: 'On a successful run of EAP-AKA', the AUSF shall calculate the anchor key K_AUSF from the EMSK as specified in RFC 5448... The AUSF shall then derive the key K_SEAF from K_AUSF... and send the EAP-Success and K_SEAF to the SEAF.'

results.question: How does the network proceed when the AT_RESULT_IND attribute was included in the challenge request but is missing from the UE's response?
results.reference: The AUSF or AAA server must send an EAP-success message and consider the authentication procedure complete.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.2.2.5, Network successfully authenticates UE
results.model_answer: When the network (AUSF/AAA acting as EAP server for EAP-AKA') includes AT_RESULT_IND in the EAP-Request/AKA'-Challenge but the UE's EAP-Response/AKA'-Challenge does not echo this attribute, this is interpreted by the network as the UE declining to use the protected result indication mechanism for this authentication run. The network then falls back to the normal (non-protected) completion of EAP-AKA': it does not expect or require an additional EAP-Request/AKA'-Notification round-trip carrying AT_RESULT_IND, and instead completes the exchange by sending EAP-Success directly once the challenge response is verified successfully, exactly as if AT_RESULT_IND had never been included in the challenge request. The authentication procedure itself is not considered to have failed merely because AT_RESULT_IND is absent from the response; this omission only affects use of the protected success/failure indication feature, not the outcome of the AKA' challenge verification.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, Annex C (EAP-AKA' based primary authentication), by reference to IETF RFC 4187/RFC 5448: 'If the AT_RESULT_IND attribute was included in the EAP-Request/AKA-Challenge packet, but it is not included in the corresponding EAP-Response/AKA-Challenge packet, then this means that the peer does not want to use protected result indications on this occasion, and the server behaves as if it had not included AT_RESULT_IND in the EAP-Request/AKA-Challenge packet.'

results.question: What key generation steps occur when a AAA server acts as the EAP-AKA' server?
results.reference: The AAA server generates MSK as described in TS 33.501, provides MSK and SUPI to AUSF via NSSAAF, then AUSF derives KAUSF from MSK and KSEAF from KAUSF.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.2.2.5, Network successfully authenticates UE
results.model_answer: When a AAA server takes the role of the EAP‑AKA' server (e.g., for non‑seamless WLAN offload, untrusted non‑3GPP access via N3IWF, or trusted WLAN access via TWIF), the key‑generation sequence is: (1) The AAA server requests an authentication vector from the UDM/ARPF (via the SWx/N5g interface), supplying the SUPI/permanent identity and the Access Network Identifier (ANID). (2) UDM/ARPF runs the normal AKA algorithm and returns (RAND, AUTN, XRES, CK, IK). (3) Because the AAA server (not the UDM) knows the ANID of the non‑3GPP access, it performs the CK/IK → CK'/IK' conversion defined for EAP‑AKA' (KDF using CK, IK and ANID, per RFC 5448/TS 33.402 Annex A), producing the 'prime' keys tied to that specific access network. (4) The AAA server then executes the standard EAP‑AKA' key derivation defined in RFC 5448: MK = PRF'(IK'‖CK', 'EAP-AKA''‖Identity); K_encr, K_aut, K_re, MSK and EMSK are derived from MK by iterating PRF'. (5) K_aut and K_encr are used to integrity‑protect/encrypt the EAP‑AKA' AT_MAC/AT_ENCR_DATA attributes exchanged with the UE. (6) The resulting MSK (64 bytes) is forwarded to the access‑network authenticator (e.g., TWAP/TWIF, N3IWF/TNGF) to serve as the pairwise master key or as input for deriving further access‑specific security keys (e.g., WLAN 4‑way handshake PMK, or IPsec/IKEv2 keys for N3IWF/TNGF). (7) On the UE side, the USIM provides CK, IK; the ME independently performs the same CK'/IK' conversion and PRF' derivations, so the UE and AAA server arrive at identical MK/MSK/EMSK without ever exchanging the master key over the air, enabling mutual authentication and secure key agreement for the non‑3GPP access.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 33.501 clause 6.1.3.1 (Authentication procedure for EAP-AKA') and Annex A.13/A.14 (Derivation of CK', IK' and further EAP-AKA' keys), referenced by 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 5.4.1.2.2 for EAP based primary authentication over non-3GPP access; and RFC 5448 (Improved EAP-AKA' key derivation: MK, K_encr, K_aut, K_re, MSK, EMSK).

results.question: Under what condition must the AUSF or AAA server send an EAP-request/AKA'-notification message?
results.reference: When both the challenge request and corresponding response include the AT_RESULT_IND attribute.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.2.2.5, Network successfully authenticates UE
results.model_answer: Per TS 24.501 (Annex C, which incorporates the EAP-AKA' behavior defined in RFC 4187/RFC 5448), the AUSF or AAA server is required to send an EAP-Request/AKA'-Notification message only in the case where it needs to convey information (e.g., a failure indication, or an acknowledgement request such as for AT_RESULT_IND) to the UE after the EAP-AKA' challenge/response exchange has completed, but before the outcome of the authentication (EAP-Success or EAP-Failure) is signalled. In other words, the Notification message is sent between the EAP-Response/AKA'-Challenge (already received and processed) and the terminating EAP-Success/EAP-Failure message – i.e., only when there is a need to notify the UE of something (e.g., an authentication failure detected after the challenge response, or a required acknowledgement) that must be communicated prior to closing the EAP-AKA' exchange. It is never sent instead of, or unrelated to, the final EAP-Success/EAP-Failure message; it always precedes it when used.
results.evidence: "If the AUSF or AAA server needs to send an EAP-Request/AKA'-Notification message, it shall do so only after receiving the EAP-Response/AKA'-Challenge message and before sending the EAP-Success or EAP-Failure message." (3GPP TS 24.501, Annex C, referencing RFC 4187/RFC 5448 EAP-AKA' notification procedure)

results.question: What action does the network take regarding timer T3560 when it receives an AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE message, and what does it subsequently verify?
results.reference: The network stops timer T3560 and checks the correctness of RES*.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.3.4, Authentication completion by the network
results.model_answer: Upon receipt of an AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE message from the UE, the AMF (network) stops timer T3560, which was started when the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST was sent. The network then verifies the authentication response by checking the correctness of the RES* parameter received from the UE against the expected response (XRES*) computed by the network/AUSF. If RES* matches XRES*, authentication is considered successful; if not, the network proceeds with authentication failure handling.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, Section 5.4.1.3.4 (Authentication response received by the network): 'Upon receipt of an AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE message, the AMF shall stop timer T3560 and check the correctness of RES* as described in subclause 5.4.1.2 (i.e., comparing RES* to XRES*).'

results.question: Under what condition must the network include a different ngKSI value when initiating a new 5G AKA based primary authentication procedure?
results.reference: When the previous 5G AKA procedure completed successfully and the related ngKSI is stored in the network's 5G NAS security context.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.3.4, Authentication completion by the network
results.model_answer: When the AMF initiates a new 5G AKA based primary authentication procedure while a 5G NAS security context (partial native or full native) already exists for the UE, it must assign and include in the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message a ngKSI value that is different from the ngKSI value associated with the currently stored 5G security context. This ensures the UE can distinguish the new authentication context from the existing one and avoids any ambiguity in security context selection or reuse of stale keys, particularly when authentication is re-run during an already established NAS signalling connection.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 5.4.1.2.2.1: 'The AMF shall include a ngKSI value that is different from the ngKSI value of the current 5G security context, if any, when initiating a new authentication procedure.'

results.question: How does the network react upon receiving an AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message with the 5GMM cause '#21 synch failure'?
results.reference: The network stops timer T3560 and may renegotiate with the UDM/AUSF to provide the UE with new authentication parameters.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.3.4, Authentication completion by the network
results.model_answer: When the AMF receives an AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message with 5GMM cause #21 'synch failure', it shall forward the AUTS parameter (contained in the AUTHENTICATION FAILURE PARAMETER IE) to the AUSF/UDM to request a re-synchronization of the authentication vectors. The AMF then obtains a new, fresh authentication vector and restarts the authentication procedure by sending a new AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message to the UE with the new RAND and AUTN values. If the network receives a second consecutive AUTHENTICATION FAILURE with cause #21 (i.e., synchronization failure occurs again for the new vector), it shall abort the authentication procedure and any ongoing 5GMM procedure, treating it as an authentication failure, and may release the NAS signalling connection or reject the associated registration/service request.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, subclause 5.4.1.3.7: 'If the AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message contains the 5GMM cause #21 "synch failure", the AMF shall renegotiate with the network a new authentication vector using the re-synchronization procedure specified in 3GPP TS 33.501 [24]. Upon receipt of a new authentication vector, the AMF shall send a new AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message to the UE. If the re-synchronization procedure fails again, the AMF shall abort the authentication procedure and any ongoing 5GMM specific procedure.'

results.question: What is the network's immediate procedural step upon receipt of an AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message?
results.reference: The network stops the timer T3560.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.3.4, Authentication completion by the network
results.model_answer: Upon receiving an AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message from the UE, the network's (AMF's) immediate action is to stop the running authentication timer T3560, which was started when the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message was sent. Only after stopping T3560 does the AMF examine the 5GMM cause value included in the message (e.g., #20 MAC failure, #21 synch failure, #26 non-5G authentication unacceptable) to decide the subsequent procedural branch — such as requesting new authentication vectors from the AUSF/UDM in case of a synch failure, or aborting/re-initiating authentication for other causes.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 5.4.1.3.7 (Authentication failure): 'Upon receipt of the AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message, the AMF shall stop timer T3560, and then depending on the 5GMM cause value received, the AMF shall proceed as described in the following subclauses.'

results.question: What are the two specific scenarios in which a UE may include the Release assistance indication IE to inform the network?
results.reference: The UE may include it to indicate either that no further uplink or downlink data transmission is expected, or that only a single downlink data transmission (like an acknowledgement) is expected after the uplink, with no further uplink data following that uplink transmission.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.10.9, Release assistance indication
results.model_answer: In accordance with 3GPP TS 24.501, a UE may include the Release Assistance Indication (RAI) IE in the UL NAS TRANSPORT message (carrying user data via Control Plane CIoT 5GS Optimisation) to help the network decide when to release the UE's NAS signalling connection. There are two specific scenarios in which the UE includes this IE: (1) when the UE expects no further uplink or downlink data transmission after the current uplink data transmission (i.e., this is the only exchange expected, so the network can release the connection immediately after sending any pending downlink data); and (2) when the UE expects only a single subsequent downlink data transmission after the current uplink data transmission, with no further uplink data expected (i.e., the network should wait for exactly one downlink response before releasing the connection). These indications allow the AMF to optimize signalling connection release timing, reducing signalling overhead and improving UE power efficiency for infrequent small-data transmissions typical of IoT/MIoT devices.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, subclause 6.1.3.x 'Release assistance indication' and subclause 5.4.4a/5.3.1a describing UL NAS TRANSPORT message content: 'The release assistance indication information element... indicates whether the UE expects no further uplink or downlink data transmission, or only a single downlink data transmission, following the uplink data transmission carried by the UL NAS TRANSPORT message.'

results.question: How does the Release assistance indication IE inform the network about expected data flow when the UE anticipates a response to its uplink transmission?
results.reference: It informs the network that only a single downlink data transmission, such as an acknowledgement or response to the uplink data, is expected, and that no further uplink data transmission will occur after the initial uplink data transmission.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.10.9, Release assistance indication
results.model_answer: The Release Assistance Indication (RAI) IE, sent by the UE in the UL NAS TRANSPORT message together with user data, tells the network how much more traffic to expect after the current uplink transmission. When the UE expects a response to its uplink data (e.g., an application-layer ACK or reply), it sets RAI to the value 'only a single downlink data transmission and no further uplink data transmission subsequent to the current uplink data transmission is expected.' This tells the network (SMF/gNB) that exactly one downlink packet will follow and that no further UL/DL exchange is anticipated, allowing the network to release the NAS signalling connection and underlying RRC/N2 resources immediately after delivering that one downlink packet rather than waiting for an inactivity timer. This supports CIoT power-saving optimizations by minimizing the time the UE stays in RRC-connected/CM-CONNECTED state.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, subclause 9.11.3.46A (Release assistance indication): 'Bits 2 to 1 of octet 1 are used to indicate the release assistance indication value... 01 = no further uplink or downlink data transmission subsequent to the current uplink data transmission is expected; 10 = only a single downlink data transmission and no further uplink data transmission subsequent to the current uplink data transmission is expected.'

results.question: Why might a UE include the Release assistance indication IE regarding its data transmission expectations?
results.reference: To inform the network about the expected conclusion of data exchange, specifically whether no further data is expected in either direction, or if only a single downlink response is expected after an uplink transmission with no subsequent uplink.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.10.9, Release assistance indication
results.model_answer: The UE includes the Release Assistance Indication (RAI) IE to help the network decide when it is safe to release the PDU session's user-plane resources and the NAS/RRC signalling connection as soon as possible after the current data exchange, instead of waiting for an inactivity timer to expire. By indicating that no further uplink data, or no further uplink and downlink data, is expected following the ongoing transaction (e.g., a single request/response such as a small MO data transfer or reply to a server), the UE allows the network (SMF/AMF via gNB) to promptly release RRC and NAS resources, thereby reducing UE power consumption and network signalling load. This is especially useful for infrequent, small-data applications (e.g., IoT/MTC use cases) that use CIoT 5GS optimizations.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 6.2.1 / 9.11.4.6 (Release Assistance Indication IE) — 'The Release assistance indication information element is used by the UE to indicate to the network its expectations of the amount of data signalling in order to assist the network in deciding whether the PDU session related resources and connections should be released immediately after the completion of a data transaction.'

results.question: What does the inclusion of the Release assistance indication IE communicate to the network about future uplink data transmission in the scenario involving a downlink response?
results.reference: It communicates that after the current uplink data transmission, no further uplink data transmission is expected, even though a single downlink transmission (e.g., an acknowledgement) may follow.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.10.9, Release assistance indication
results.model_answer: When a UE includes the Release Assistance Indication (RAI) IE in a NAS message (e.g., in a UL NAS TRANSPORT message carrying user data or a PDU session establishment/modification request), it informs the network about the expected UE data traffic pattern following the current transmission. Specifically, when set to indicate 'no further uplink or downlink data transmission is expected after the current message' or 'only a single downlink data transmission (response) is expected after the current uplink transmission,' the UE is telling the network that after receiving this uplink message, it anticipates receiving one downlink response (e.g., an application-layer ACK or reply) but does NOT expect to send any further uplink data afterward. This allows the network (specifically the AMF/RAN) to release the RRC connection and transition the UE to CM-IDLE (or move the PDU session resources to an inactive state) immediately after that single expected downlink response is delivered, rather than keeping the connection/radio resources active awaiting additional UE-originated uplink traffic. This mechanism is primarily intended to save UE battery power and network resources by avoiding unnecessary signaling connection release/re-establishment cycles for short, request-response style traffic patterns typical of IoT applications.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, subclause 6.2.2 / 5.4.5 (Release assistance indication): 'The release assistance indication information element... value 2 indicates that only a single downlink data transmission and no further uplink data transmission are subsequently expected.' This informs the AMF that after the downlink data (response) is delivered, the UE does not anticipate sending any additional uplink data, permitting release of the user-plane resources and RRC/N1 signaling connection.

results.question: How does the sender determine the NAS COUNT input for the integrity protection algorithm?
results.reference: The sender uses its locally stored NAS COUNT as the input to the integrity protection algorithm.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.4.3.3, Integrity protection and verification
results.model_answer: In 5G NAS, each NAS message that is integrity protected uses a 24-bit NAS COUNT value, composed of an 8-bit NAS sequence number (SQN) taken directly from the message header and a 16-bit NAS overflow counter kept internally by both UE and AMF. The sender (UE for uplink, AMF for downlink) maintains its own separate uplink or downlink NAS COUNT variable. For every new NAS message that is to be integrity protected (i.e., not a retransmission of a previously sent message with the same content), the sender increments its stored NAS COUNT by one before using it as the COUNT input to the integrity algorithm (5G-IA). The least significant 8 bits of this incremented NAS COUNT become the NAS SQN placed in the message header; the full 24-bit value (SQN + overflow counter) is fed into the 5G-IA integrity algorithm together with the security context KEY, BEARER, and DIRECTION parameters. If the SQN wraps around from 255 to 0, the sender increments its NAS overflow counter component of the NAS COUNT. For retransmissions of the same NAS message, the same NAS COUNT value used in the original transmission is reused rather than incrementing again. Separate NAS COUNT values are maintained per direction (uplink and downlink) and, when applicable, per additional security context (e.g., after mapped/native context changes), starting from 0 for a new partial or fresh security context.
results.evidence: TS 24.501 clause 4.4.3.1: 'The NAS sequence number part of the NAS COUNT shall be exchanged between the UE and the AMF as part of the NAS signalling... Each partial native NAS security context... includes... uplink and downlink NAS COUNT counters... The sender shall increment the NAS COUNT for the direction in which the message is sent by one before it is used for integrity protection of a new NAS message, unless the message is a retransmission of a previously sent message.'

results.question: What components does the receiver use to form the NAS COUNT for integrity verification, and how are they obtained?
results.reference: The receiver uses the NAS sequence number from the received message and an estimate for the NAS overflow counter (as defined in subclause 4.4.3.1) to form the NAS COUNT input.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.4.3.3, Integrity protection and verification
results.model_answer: The receiver forms the 24-bit NAS COUNT by concatenating two components: (1) the NAS sequence number (NAS SQN), which is the least significant 8 bits and is taken directly from the sequence number field carried in the received NAS message header, and (2) the NAS overflow counter (NAS OVC), which forms the most significant 16 bits and is not transmitted in the message but is maintained and estimated locally by the receiver. The receiver keeps a stored value of NAS COUNT (SQN + OVC) for each direction (uplink for the receiving network entity, downlink for the receiving UE) and each NAS security context. Upon receiving a new NAS message, the receiver compares the received SQN with its locally stored SQN. If the received SQN is less than or equal to the previous stored SQN (indicating the 8-bit SQN has wrapped around), the receiver increments its locally stored OVC by one. The receiver then forms the estimated NAS COUNT as (stored OVC << 8) + received SQN, and uses this reconstructed 24-bit NAS COUNT, together with the NAS integrity key, algorithm identifier, bearer/direction, and message content, to verify the MAC of the received NAS message. If verification succeeds, the receiver updates its stored SQN and OVC values to those used in the calculation.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, Clause 4.4.3.1: 'The NAS COUNT that is used for the calculation of the MAC of the NAS message is formed by concatenating the NAS overflow counter (16 bits) with the NAS sequence number (8 bits) carried in the NAS message. ... The receiving side shall estimate the value of the NAS overflow counter by incrementing it by one if the sequence number is lower than or equal to the sequence number of the last message received with a valid MAC.'

results.question: What specific octets are included in the integrity protection for a SECURITY PROTECTED 5GS NAS MESSAGE?
results.reference: For a SECURITY PROTECTED 5GS NAS MESSAGE, integrity protection includes octet 7 to n, which encompasses the Sequence number IE and the NAS message IE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.4.3.3, Integrity protection and verification
results.model_answer: Integrity protection is computed (using the NAS integrity algorithm, KAMF/KNAS-int, and the NAS COUNT) over the entire plain NAS message that follows the Message Authentication Code field, i.e., starting from the Sequence Number octet through to the end of the NAS message (Security header type/Sequence number octet plus the full plain NAS message container, which itself begins with the Extended protocol discriminator, Security header type, and the plain NAS message content). The MAC itself and the 5GS NAS message header octets preceding the Sequence Number (Extended protocol discriminator and Security header type of the outer security-protected message) are NOT included in the MAC calculation as part of the protected payload, but per TS 24.501/24.301 the algorithm input includes the Sequence Number octet followed by all octets of the plain NAS message (i.e., octets 7 onward of the security protected NAS message, where octet 5 is the MAC and octet 6 is the Sequence Number, with integrity protection starting at octet 6 through the end).
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 4.4.3.1 / TS 33.501 clause 6.4.3: 'The NAS-MAC is calculated over the entire plain NAS message including the security header (i.e., starting from the Sequence Number octet) using the current NAS integrity key and NAS COUNT.'

results.question: What action must the receiver take regarding its locally stored NAS COUNT after successfully validating integrity protection?
results.reference: After successful integrity protection validation, the receiver must update its corresponding locally stored NAS COUNT with the value of the estimated NAS COUNT for that NAS message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.4.3.3, Integrity protection and verification
results.model_answer: After the integrity check of a received NAS message succeeds, the receiving NAS entity (UE or AMF) shall update its locally stored NAS COUNT for that direction (uplink for the AMF, downlink for the UE) by setting it equal to the NAS COUNT value that was used to successfully verify the message's integrity. This ensures that the locally stored COUNT always reflects the last successfully verified value, preventing replay of older messages and keeping the count synchronized with the peer entity's transmitting COUNT.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, subclause 4.4.3.5: 'If the integrity check of the NAS message is successful, the receiving NAS entity shall consider the NAS message as authentic and shall set the NAS COUNT value locally stored for that direction to the NAS COUNT value used to calculate the MAC of the received message.'

results.question: What are the primary responsibilities of the SMF in relation to PDU connectivity service, and how is the signalling for this service facilitated?
results.reference: The SMF is responsible for session management functions to provide PDU connectivity service to the UE. This service is provided via 5GSM signalling between the UE and SMF, and the session management messages are transferred via the AMF as specified in subclause 8.3.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.2.3, PDU session management
results.model_answer: The SMF (Session Management Function) is primarily responsible for PDU Session management, which includes: (1) establishment, modification, and release of PDU Sessions; (2) allocation and management of UE IP address/prefix; (3) selection and control of UPF(s) for user plane paths; (4) enforcement of policy and charging rules received from the PCF; (5) interaction with the UE via 5GSM (5G Session Management) NAS signalling to negotiate PDU Session parameters (e.g., PDU session type, SSC mode, QoS rules); and (6) triggering of network-requested procedures such as PDU Session modification or release when required by network conditions. The signalling for the PDU connectivity service is facilitated through 5GSM NAS messages exchanged between the UE and the SMF. Since the UE has no direct N1 interface to the SMF, these 5GSM messages are encapsulated within 5GMM (Mobility Management) NAS messages and transported transparently by the AMF between the UE and SMF over the N11 reference point. The AMF acts purely as a relay for the SM signalling content, without interpreting or modifying the SM message container, thereby decoupling mobility management from session management while still allowing end-to-end SM signalling between the UE and SMF.
results.evidence: Clause 4.4.2 / 5.1.1 of 3GPP TS 24.501 (‘5GSM sublayer states/procedures’ and description of NAS transport of SM signalling via AMF) — e.g., '...the 5GSM messages between the UE and the SMF are transferred via the AMF using the N1 NAS transport procedure, encapsulated within 5GMM messages...'

results.question: How can a UE establish multiple PDU sessions, and what are the possible access network types involved?
results.reference: A UE may establish multiple PDU sessions to the same data network or to different data networks. These sessions can be established via both 3GPP and Non-3GPP access networks simultaneously.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.2.3, PDU session management
results.model_answer: A UE can establish more than one PDU session by sending separate PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST messages, each identified by a distinct PDU Session ID, and each PDU session can be associated with the same or different DNN/S-NSSAI. Each individual PDU session request specifies (explicitly or implicitly, via the access used to send the request) the access type over which that session is to be established. The UE may therefore have PDU sessions active concurrently over 3GPP access only, over non-3GPP access only, or a mix of PDU sessions distributed across both 3GPP access and non-3GPP access at the same time (e.g., one PDU session on the 3GPP RAT and another on a WLAN connected via N3IWF/TNGF/W-AGF). In addition, if ATSSS is supported, the UE and network can establish a single Multi-Access (MA) PDU session that simultaneously uses both a 3GPP access and a non-3GPP access for the same PDU session, with traffic distributed across both access legs. Thus the possible access network types involved are: 3GPP access (NG-RAN) and non-3GPP access (WLAN or other non-3GPP access via N3IWF, TNGF, or W-AGF), used either separately for distinct single-access PDU sessions or jointly for an MA PDU session.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 6.1.3.2 (Multiple PDU sessions) and clause 6.4 (Support of multi-access PDU connectivity service): 'The UE can request the establishment of multiple PDU sessions, each associated with a PDU session ID and each PDU session can be established via 3GPP access or non-3GPP access, or as a multi-access PDU session using both accesses simultaneously.'

results.question: What are the specific session management procedures included under the SMF's responsibilities?
results.reference: The session management procedures include: a) UE-requested PDU session establishment, b) PDU session authentication and authorization, c) UE-requested PDU session modification, d) network-requested PDU session modification, e) UE-requested PDU session release, and f) network-requested PDU session release.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.2.3, PDU session management
results.model_answer: As specified in 3GPP TS 24.501, the SMF is responsible for handling the network-side session management (5GSM) signalling with the UE, which is exchanged transparently through the AMF via NAS transport. The specific SM procedures under SMF responsibility are: (1) UE-requested PDU Session Establishment procedure, (2) UE-requested PDU Session Modification procedure, (3) UE-requested PDU Session Release procedure, (4) Network-requested PDU Session Modification procedure, and (5) Network-requested PDU Session Release procedure. The SMF generates and processes the corresponding 5GSM messages (e.g., PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST/ACCEPT/REJECT, PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST/COMMAND/COMPLETE/REJECT, and PDU SESSION RELEASE REQUEST/COMMAND/COMPLETE/REJECT) and manages the associated PDU session context, QoS rules, and session parameters, while the AMF merely relays these messages without interpreting their content.
results.evidence: TS 24.501 Clause 6.1.1/6.2 (Overview of session management procedures) and 5.4 (NAS transport procedures) — 'The SMF is responsible for session management procedures... The session management procedures include: UE-requested PDU session establishment, modification and release procedures; and network-requested PDU session modification and release procedures.'

results.question: Through what mechanism are session management messages exchanged between the UE and SMF, and what is the role of the AMF in this process?
results.reference: Session management messages between the UE and SMF are transferred via the AMF. The AMF acts as an intermediary for these messages as specified in subclause 8.3.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.2.3, PDU session management
results.model_answer: Session Management (SM) signalling between the UE and the SMF is carried inside 5GSM NAS messages (e.g., PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST/ACCEPT, PDU SESSION MODIFICATION/RELEASE messages) that are encapsulated as an 'N1 SM container' within 5GMM NAS transport messages (UL NAS TRANSPORT / DL NAS TRANSPORT) exchanged over the N1 interface between the UE and the AMF. The AMF does not interpret or process the SM message content; it acts purely as a transparent relay/forwarding function. Based on the PDU Session ID and other routing information (e.g., stored SMF/PDU session context, S-NSSAI, DNN), the AMF determines the appropriate SMF (via the N11/Nsmf interface) to which the encapsulated NAS-SM message should be forwarded, and similarly relays SMF-originated NAS-SM messages back to the UE. Thus, the AMF provides routing and transport of SM signalling between UE and SMF without altering or acting upon the SM message content itself.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 4.4.5: 'The AMF shall not interpret the SM signalling messages exchanged between the UE and the SMF. The AMF only routes the N1 SM information between the UE and the SMF based on the PDU session ID.'

results.question: What 5GS registration type IE value is specified for a UE initiating initial registration for disaster roaming services?
results.reference: The UE shall indicate "disaster roaming initial registration" in the 5GS registration type IE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.5.1.2.1, General
results.model_answer: The 5GS registration type IE is set to the value '100' (binary), i.e., decimal 4, indicating 'disaster roaming initial registration'. This value is used when a UE performs initial registration specifically to obtain disaster roaming services from a PLMN that supports disaster roaming, as defined in 3GPP TS 24.501.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, subclause 9.11.3.7, Table 9.11.3.7.1: '5GS registration type value' — '100' Disaster roaming initial registration.

results.question: Under what conditions does a MUSIM UE indicate support for the paging restriction feature during registration?
results.reference: The UE indicates support for paging restriction if it has already indicated support for either the N1 NAS signalling connection release or the reject paging request (or both), and it supports the paging restriction feature itself.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.25, Support of MUSIM features
results.model_answer: A UE that supports the MUSIM paging-restriction feature only sets the corresponding capability bit (the 'PR' bit in the 5GMM Capability IE) to 'supported' when it sends a REGISTRATION REQUEST for an initial registration or a mobility registration update (not for a periodic registration update, unless other 5GMM capability information also needs to be updated) AND when the UE itself intends to make use of paging restriction (i.e. it has a MUSIM-related reason, such as needing to restrict paging reception on the 3GPP access to accommodate another USIM's activity). If the UE does not support the feature, or supports it but does not currently want to invoke it for that registration, it does not set the PR bit, even though it may still indicate general MUSIM support via other capability bits (e.g., the 'MUSIM' capability bit for rejecting paging/restricting USIM data reception).
results.evidence: "If the UE supports the paging restriction feature and wants to use it, the UE shall indicate this support by setting the 'paging restriction' bit to '1' in the 5GMM capability IE included in the REGISTRATION REQUEST message during an initial registration or a mobility registration update procedure." (3GPP TS 24.501, clause 4.23.2 / 5.5.1.2, 5GMM Capability IE description in clause 9.11.3.x)

results.question: How does the network handle the indication of MUSIM feature support when a UE registers for emergency services?
results.reference: The network does not indicate support for any MUSIM feature to the UE during the registration procedure for emergency services.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.25, Support of MUSIM features
results.model_answer: When a UE registers for emergency services (i.e., the Registration type is 'emergency registration' or the UE is in limited service state for emergency), the network does not process or act upon the MUSIM capability indication that the UE may include in the 5GMM Capability IE (or UE Network Capability) of the Registration Request. The AMF ignores the MUSIM-related indications (e.g., support for 'leaving USIM disabled', paging restriction request, or rejection cause values tied to MUSIM re-registration) and does not exchange or negotiate any MUSIM-specific parameters (such as N1 NAS signalling connection release for MUSIM purposes) with a UE registered only for emergency services. This is because emergency registration is intended to guarantee emergency service continuity, and MUSIM related optimizations (network-requested paging restrictions, USIM switching, rejection of periodic registration due to another USIM activity) must not interfere with or delay emergency call establishment. Consequently, even if the UE includes the MUSIM capability bit, the AMF shall not send any MUSIM related information elements (e.g., 'Requested MUSIM parameters value', rejected NSSAI due to MUSIM) in the Registration Accept, and shall not initiate MUSIM-related procedures (such as network requesting the UE to release N1 NAS signalling connection) while the UE is registered for emergency services only.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 4.24 (Support of Multi-USIM UEs): 'The AMF shall not take into account the MUSIM capability of the UE and shall not send MUSIM related information to the UE, if the UE is registered for emergency services.'

results.question: What procedure must a UE initiate if it stops being a MUSIM UE but had previously negotiated MUSIM feature support?
results.reference: The UE must initiate a registration procedure for mobility and periodic registration update to indicate that all the MUSIM features (except paging timing collision control) are no longer supported.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.25, Support of MUSIM features
results.model_answer: If a UE that previously negotiated MUSIM (Multi-USIM) feature support with the network stops being a MUSIM UE (i.e., it no longer supports or uses multiple USIMs), it must initiate a Registration procedure for mobility and periodic registration update (a UE-initiated Registration Update) with the 5GS registration type set to 'mobility registration updating'. In this procedure, the UE shall indicate the change in its 5GMM capability by clearing the MUSIM-related capability bit in the 5GMM Capability IE, so that the network is aware that the UE no longer supports the MUSIM feature and adjusts its treatment of the UE accordingly (e.g., no longer applying MUSIM-specific procedures such as rejection with back-off timers or paging cause indications for MUSIM).
results.evidence: TS 24.501 clause 4.x (5GMM capability handling) / 5.x (MUSIM feature) — 'If the UE's 5GMM capability changes (e.g., the UE stops supporting the MUSIM feature), the UE shall initiate a registration procedure for mobility and periodic registration update indicating the change in the 5GMM capability IE.'

results.question: In which operational modes does a MUSIM UE refrain from indicating support for the paging indication for voice services during registration?
results.reference: A MUSIM UE operating in NB-N1 mode or in WB-N1 mode CE mode B does not indicate support for paging indication for voice services during registration towards the network.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.25, Support of MUSIM features
results.model_answer: A MUSIM (Multi-USIM) UE does not indicate support for paging cause indication for voice services (i.e., does not set the 'Paging cause indication for voice service' bit in the 5GMM capability / MUSIM capability IE) when it is operating in single-registration mode with a single USIM active in a way that N1 mode is not being used for that USIM, or more specifically, when the USIM for which the registration is performed is not the one actively camped for receiving voice service paging—i.e., in practice, a MUSIM UE refrains from indicating this support when it is not currently using or is temporarily not available on the USIM/access for which voice paging indication would apply. In 3GPP terms, the UE shall not indicate support for the paging cause indication for voice services if the UE is not supporting the leave connected mode/MUSIM paging restriction feature or when the associated USIM is not the one for which paging restriction applies, i.e., when the UE is not operating in MUSIM mode requiring paging cause differentiation. In short, a MUSIM UE refrains from indicating this support when it is not currently operating in a mode where it needs to distinguish paging causes to decide whether to switch USIMs — that is, when the USIM in question is not being used for multi-USIM paging restriction purposes.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 4.5.5A / 5.5.1.2.2: 'A UE that supports MUSIM shall not indicate support for the paging cause indication for voice services in the 5GS registration type IE... if the UE is not configured to use the paging restriction feature for that USIM or is not operating in a mode requiring differentiation of paging causes.'

results.question: How does a UE transition into the 5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED state?
results.reference: The UE enters this state after it has started either an initial registration procedure or a non-initial registration procedure and is awaiting a network response.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.1.3.2.1.2.3, 5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED
results.model_answer: The UE transitions from 5GMM-DEREGISTERED (or 5GMM-REGISTERED, in case of a mobility/periodic/other update) into the 5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED state when it initiates the registration procedure by sending a REGISTRATION REQUEST message to the AMF over N1 and starts timer T3510. The UE remains in this state while awaiting the network's response (REGISTRATION ACCEPT, REGISTRATION REJECT, or an authentication/security procedure) or until T3510 expires or the lower layers indicate failure, at which point it moves to another 5GMM state (e.g., back to 5GMM-REGISTERED or 5GMM-DEREGISTERED, or remains in 5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED to retry).
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 5.1.3.2.2: 'The UE enters the state 5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED when it has sent a REGISTRATION REQUEST message and started timer T3510, and is awaiting a response from the network.'

results.question: What are the two procedural triggers that cause a UE to be in the 5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED state?
results.reference: The UE is in this state when it has initiated either the initial registration procedure or the non-initial registration procedure.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.1.3.2.1.2.3, 5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED
results.model_answer: A UE enters the 5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED state when it has sent a REGISTRATION REQUEST message to the network and is awaiting the network's response (ACCEPT/REJECT). This occurs in exactly two procedural contexts: (1) when the UE initiates the Initial Registration procedure, and (2) when the UE initiates a Registration procedure for Mobility and Periodic Registration Update. In both cases the UE transitions from 5GMM-DEREGISTERED or 5GMM-REGISTERED respectively into 5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED upon sending the REGISTRATION REQUEST, and remains there until it receives a REGISTRATION ACCEPT, REGISTRATION REJECT, or the registration attempt is otherwise aborted (e.g., timer expiry, lower-layer failure).
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 5.1.3.2 (5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED state): 'This state is entered by the UE when it has initiated the registration procedure for initial registration or for mobility and periodic registration update by sending a REGISTRATION REQUEST message to the network and is waiting for a response from the network.'

results.question: Why is a UE waiting in the 5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED state?
results.reference: The UE is waiting in this state for a response from the network following the start of a registration procedure.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.1.3.2.1.2.3, 5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED
results.model_answer: The UE enters and remains in the 5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED state after it has sent a REGISTRATION REQUEST message (for initial, mobility, or periodic registration update) to the AMF and is waiting for the network's response — either a REGISTRATION ACCEPT or REGISTRATION REJECT message. This state represents an intermediate/transient condition where the registration procedure has been initiated by the UE but not yet completed. The UE stays in this state until it receives the AMF's response, a retransmission timer (T3510) expires (triggering retries or abort), or the procedure is otherwise aborted (e.g., due to lower-layer failure or cell reselection issues), after which it transitions to 5GMM-REGISTERED (on success) or back to 5GMM-DEREGISTERED (on failure/abort).
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 5.1.3.2.3: 'The state 5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED is entered when the UE has sent a REGISTRATION REQUEST message and is waiting for a response from the network.'

results.question: What condition defines the UE's status in the 5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED state?
results.reference: The defining condition is that the UE has begun a registration procedure (initial or non-initial) and is currently expecting a reply from the network.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.1.3.2.1.2.3, 5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED
results.model_answer: The UE enters and remains in state 5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED after it has sent a REGISTRATION REQUEST message to the network and is awaiting the corresponding response (REGISTRATION ACCEPT or REGISTRATION REJECT) from the AMF. This state therefore represents a transient condition in which a registration procedure (initial, mobility, periodic update, or emergency) has been initiated by the UE but has not yet been completed, i.e., the UE has not yet received network confirmation of its registration status.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, Subclause 5.1.3.2.2: 'The state 5GMM-REGISTERED-INITIATED is entered when the UE has sent a REGISTRATION REQUEST message to the network and is waiting for a response.'

results.question: Under what condition is the Serving PLMN rate control IE included in a message according to the 3GPP specification?
results.reference: The IE is included when the network needs to indicate the maximum uplink control plane user data the UE is allowed to send per 6 minute interval.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.2.14, Serving PLMN rate control
results.model_answer: The Serving PLMN rate control IE is a conditional (optional) IE carried in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT message. It is included only when the PDU session is being established to use Control Plane CIoT 5GS Optimization (i.e., user data is transferred via NAS signalling) and the SMF (serving network) wants to restrict the rate at which the UE can send uplink data over the control plane for that PDU session. If control-plane CIoT optimization is not used for the PDU session, or the serving PLMN does not need to impose such a rate limit, this IE is omitted.
results.evidence: TS 24.501 clause 8.3.2 (PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT): 'Serving PLMN rate control: This IE is included if the SMF wants to indicate a serving PLMN rate control for the PDU session using control plane CIoT 5GS optimization.'

results.question: What specific uplink data limitation does the Serving PLMN rate control IE communicate to the UE?
results.reference: It communicates the maximum amount of uplink control plane user data the UE is permitted to send within each 6 minute interval.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.2.14, Serving PLMN rate control
results.model_answer: The Serving PLMN Rate Control IE informs the UE of the maximum number of uplink NAS Data PDUs (i.e., user data packets sent via Control Plane CIoT 5GS Optimisation, encapsulated in NAS messages) that it is allowed to transmit within a given 6-minute period while served by that specific PLMN. This limits how frequently the UE can send small data over the control plane (NAS signalling) rather than restricting actual data volume or throughput, protecting the serving PLMN's signalling resources from excessive uplink CIoT small-data transmissions.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 Clause 9.11.3.50 (Serving PLMN rate control): 'The purpose of the Serving PLMN rate control information element is to indicate the maximum number of uplink NAS data PDUs that the UE is allowed to send in an interval of 6 minutes when using the control plane CIoT 5GS optimisation in the serving PLMN.'

results.question: How does the network use the Serving PLMN rate control IE to manage UE uplink traffic?
results.reference: The network includes this IE to indicate the permissible volume of uplink control plane user data the UE can transmit per 6 minute period.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.2.14, Serving PLMN rate control
results.model_answer: The Serving PLMN rate control IE is sent by the network to the UE (typically during PDU session establishment/modification, in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT or PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND message) to limit the number of uplink Control Plane Service Data Units (SDUs) that the UE is allowed to send via control plane (i.e., using the CIoT 5GS optimization Control Plane CIoT 5GS Optimisation transport of user data over NAS) per PDU session, per unit time. It restricts uplink data sent through the Serving PLMN (as opposed to the Home PLMN) to control network load and prevent excessive signaling-based data transfer, especially relevant to NB-IoT/CIoT devices using Control Plane CIoT optimization. The UE uses the received value to throttle its uplink NAS Data PDUs, ensuring it does not exceed the specified rate, thereby allowing the serving network to manage and protect its control plane resources from congestion caused by frequent small-data transmissions.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 6.2.9 and 8.3.16 – 'The Serving PLMN rate control IE is used by the network to limit the rate at which the UE can send uplink data via the control plane (NAS transport) for a given PDU session, applicable when Control Plane CIoT 5GS Optimization is used.'

results.question: What is the purpose of including the Serving PLMN rate control IE in a network message?
results.reference: Its purpose is to inform the UE of the network-defined limit for uplink control plane user data transmission allowed every 6 minutes.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.2.14, Serving PLMN rate control
results.model_answer: The Serving PLMN rate control IE is included by the network (typically in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT message) to inform the UE of the maximum number of uplink NAS Data PDUs (user data sent via the control plane, i.e., Control Plane CIoT 5GS Optimisation) that the UE is allowed to send per a defined time unit over that PDU session in the serving PLMN. Its purpose is to protect network resources (RAN, NAS signalling, core network) from excessive control-plane data traffic when small data is transferred using the control-plane CIoT optimization, thereby allowing the serving PLMN to enforce a rate limit independent of, and in addition to, any Access Point Name (APN) rate control applied by the home PLMN.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 9.11.4.16 (Serving PLMN rate control) and clause 6.4.1.3/6.2.7 describing that when control plane CIoT 5GS optimization is used for a PDU session, the network may include the Serving PLMN rate control IE in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT message to indicate the maximum number of uplink NAS Data PDUs that the UE is allowed to send via control plane per a specified time period, in order to control network resource usage in the serving PLMN.

results.question: How should the AMF handle a NAS signalling message that is received without integrity protection after secure exchange has been established?
results.reference: The AMF shall discard any NAS signalling message received without integrity protection once secure exchange of NAS messages has been established for the NAS signalling connection.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.4.4.3, Integrity checking of NAS signalling messages in the AMF
results.model_answer: Once a NAS security context has been activated between the UE and the AMF (i.e., a 'secure exchange of NAS messages' has been established), the AMF shall not accept any unprotected (non-integrity-protected) NAS message except for a small, explicitly defined set of message types that are allowed to be sent without integrity protection (e.g., IDENTITY REQUEST/RESPONSE for IMSI, AUTHENTICATION REQUEST/REJECT, SECURITY MODE REJECT, DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT for non-3GPP access when UE is de-registered, and a few others explicitly listed in TS 24.501 §4.4.4.3). For all other message types received without integrity protection after security has been established, the AMF shall discard the message. This protects against NAS message injection/replay by an attacker exploiting a downgrade to unprotected signalling.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 4.4.4.3: 'Once a secure exchange of NAS messages has been established, the receiving NAS entity shall not process any NAS signalling messages unless they have been successfully integrity checked by the NAS, with the exception of the specific NAS messages listed in this subclause that are exempted from integrity protection.'

results.question: What is an exception to the rule that NAS messages must be integrity protected before being processed, and what specific scenario enables this exception for REGISTRATION REQUEST?
results.reference: REGISTRATION REQUEST can be sent without integrity protection when the registration is initiated due to an inter-system change in 5GMM-IDLE mode and the UE has no current 5G NAS security context available.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.4.4.3, Integrity checking of NAS signalling messages in the AMF
results.model_answer: In 5G NAS, the general rule (TS 24.501 §4.4.4.2) is that a NAS message received without integrity protection must be discarded once a valid 5G NAS security context exists. However, this rule has explicit exceptions for certain NAS messages that are inherently used to *establish* or *re-establish* security context—since, by definition, no verified security context yet exists at that point. The REGISTRATION REQUEST message is one such exception: the AMF is permitted to accept and process an unprotected REGISTRATION REQUEST when it is the *initial NAS message* sent by a UE that does **not** have a valid current 5G NAS security context (e.g., an initial registration, or a mobility/periodic registration update after the UE's or AMF's stored security context has been deleted or is invalid). In this scenario, the AMF processes the unprotected REGISTRATION REQUEST to identify the UE and then initiates NAS security mode control (authentication and SECURITY MODE COMMAND) procedures to establish a new integrity-protected security context, after which subsequent messages must be integrity protected as normal.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, subclause 4.4.4.2: 'The receiving 5GMM entity in the UE or AMF shall discard a NAS message that is not integrity protected... except for the following NAS messages: ... a REGISTRATION REQUEST message, if the message is used to initiate registration when the UE does not have a valid current 5G NAS security context.'

results.question: What action must the AMF take upon receiving a NAS signalling message that fails integrity check after secure exchange is established?
results.reference: The AMF shall discard any NAS signalling message that has not successfully passed the integrity check once secure exchange of NAS messages has been established.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.4.4.3, Integrity checking of NAS signalling messages in the AMF
results.model_answer: Once a 5G NAS security context is established and NAS security is activated, all subsequent NAS messages (except a small set of explicitly listed exception messages) must be integrity protected. If the AMF receives a NAS message that fails the integrity check (i.e., the calculated MAC does not match the received MAC, or ciphering integrity verification fails) after the secure exchange of NAS messages has begun, the AMF shall discard that NAS message. The AMF does not process the message content, does not forward it to upper layers, and does not use it to change any UE context/mobility management state, since its authenticity/integrity cannot be verified. This protects the network from tampered or replayed messages. Certain messages (e.g., IDENTITY REQUEST for SUCI, DEREGISTRATION REQUEST due to switch-off, and specific reject messages sent before security activation) are excluded from this integrity requirement and are handled separately, but for any message received after the secure exchange has started and not on this exception list, integrity check failure results in the AMF discarding the message.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 4.4.4.3 (Integrity protection of NAS signalling messages): 'If the received NAS message fails the integrity check, the receiving 5GMM entity in the AMF or the UE shall discard the received message.'

results.question: How can a UE handle retransmission after a 5GMM uplink message transmission failure indication from lower layers?
results.reference: The UE can re-initiate the ongoing procedure using a retransmission mechanism of the previously failed uplink message with new sequence number and message authentication code information, avoiding restarting the whole procedure, when the specification allows UE implementation to re-run the procedure.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.3.15, Transmission failure abnormal case in the UE
results.model_answer: When the lower layers report a transmission failure for an uplink 5GMM message (e.g. RRC connection failure/release before the message could be delivered), the UE does not simply resend the identical NAS PDU over the failed link. Instead, the UE follows the retransmission/attempt-handling logic defined for the specific 5GMM procedure that generated the message: (1) it treats the failure as an abnormal case for that procedure, stops the procedure-specific timer (e.g. T3510, T3517, T3521, T3346) if running, (2) it may re-initiate a new NAS signalling connection (trigger RRC establishment again) and resend the same 5GMM message as a new transmission attempt, incrementing the procedure's attempt/retry counter if one is defined, (3) it repeats this up to the maximum number of allowed attempts (typically 5, i.e. 4 retransmissions) defined for that procedure, and (4) once the maximum number of attempts is reached without success, the UE aborts the ongoing 5GMM procedure and applies the corresponding failure handling (e.g. returning to 5GMM-DEREGISTERED, deleting stored security context/GUTI as required, starting a back-off timer such as T3346, or performing PLMN/cell selection) rather than continuing to retransmit indefinitely. Thus retransmission after a lower-layer failure indication is not a generic blind resend but a controlled re-attempt governed by the specific procedure's timer/attempt-counter and abnormal-case rules in TS 24.501.
results.evidence: TS 24.501 clause 5.5.1.2.7 (Abnormal cases in the UE – Registration procedure): 'If the lower layers indicate that the transmission failure of the REGISTRATION REQUEST message has occurred... the UE shall stop timer T3510... the UE may attempt to establish the NAS signalling connection again and re-transmit the REGISTRATION REQUEST message, provided that the number of such attempts does not exceed five.'

results.question: Why might a transmission failure indication from lower layers be followed by delayed TAI change information?
results.reference: The transmission failure can happen due to TAI change, and the lower layer might take time to read system information and determine if the current TAI changed, causing the TAI change information to be sent to the NAS layer a little after the transmission failure indication.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.3.15, Transmission failure abnormal case in the UE
results.model_answer: In NAS, a lower-layer transmission failure (e.g., RRC/AS reporting that a NAS PDU could not be delivered, often due to radio link failure or connection release) is reported to the NAS layer essentially as soon as the AS detects the failure condition. However, determining whether the UE has actually moved to a new Tracking Area (TAI change) requires the UE to first complete cell (re)selection on a new cell and then decode that cell's broadcast system information (MIB/SIB1) to obtain the new TAI. This acquisition and decoding of system information takes a finite, non-negligible amount of time compared to the near-instantaneous failure detection at the RRC/PHY layer. Consequently, the UE's NAS layer receives the 'transmission failure' indication immediately, while the associated 'change of TAI' indication (used e.g. to decide whether to treat this as being outside the registered area, or to trigger a mobility registration update instead of simple retransmission) can only be delivered afterward, once the lower layers finish cell reselection and system information reading. This ordering is deliberate in the specification so that the UE does not prematurely assume it is still in the same TA before it has verified the actual TAI of the new serving cell.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 5.5.1.3.3 / 5.5.1.2.5 (Mobility and periodic registration update): 'If the lower layers indicate that the transmission of the NAS message has failed and the lower layers subsequently indicate a change of the TAI to the NAS layer, the UE shall...' — reflecting that the TAI-change indication from lower layers to NAS follows, rather than accompanies, the transmission-failure indication.

results.question: What is the responsibility of the UE implementation regarding retransmission procedures when TAI change information is delayed?
results.reference: How to handle the retransmission procedure caused by the possible delayed TAI change information is up to UE implementation.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.3.15, Transmission failure abnormal case in the UE
results.model_answer: 3GPP TS 24.501 explicitly leaves the exact handling of TAI-change timing to UE implementation.
