Because the lower layers may report a change of TAI to the NAS layer with some delay after the UE has actually entered a new tracking area (e.g., due to cell reselection or handover procedures at lower layers), the UE cannot always know precisely when the TAI has changed. Consequently, it is the UE implementation's responsibility to decide how to treat any NAS retransmission procedure (e.g., retransmission of REGISTRATION REQUEST, SERVICE REQUEST, or other NAS messages governed by timers such as T3510, T3517, T3540) that is in progress when such a delayed TAI-change indication is finally received. The UE must ensure that once it becomes aware of the TAI change, it applies this knowledge consistently to any pending retransmission counters/timers so that it does not keep retransmitting a NAS message tied to an outdated TAI context, while the specification itself does not mandate a fixed procedure for reconciling this delay - it is a UE implementation choice how to synchronize the delayed indication with ongoing retransmission logic.
results.evidence: NOTE: It is up to the UE implementation how to take into account the delay in the indication of a change of tracking area from the lower layers when performing NAS retransmission procedures.

results.question: Under what condition can a UE re-initiate a procedure using a retransmission mechanism after an uplink message transmission failure?
results.reference: When it is specified in the relevant procedure that it is up to the UE implementation to re-run the ongoing procedure that triggered that procedure.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.3.15, Transmission failure abnormal case in the UE
results.model_answer: A UE is only allowed to re-initiate a NAS procedure by invoking a retransmission mechanism when the lower layers explicitly report that the uplink message could not be delivered (e.g., RRC/AS layer failure, radio link failure, or lack of acknowledgement) *before* any response to that message was received from the network, and provided that (a) no NAS timer associated with that procedure is currently running (any such timer must have been stopped as a result of the failure indication), (b) the number of retransmission attempts for that message has not already reached the maximum allowed value defined for the procedure, and (c) the UE is not barred from initiating the procedure by any other condition (e.g., back-off timer, congestion control, or a 'not allowed' state). If these conditions hold, the UE may resend the same NAS message using the retransmission mechanism instead of treating the failure as an abnormal case requiring full procedure abort.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, subclause 5.5.1.2.7 (and analogous 'Abnormal cases in the UE' subclauses for other procedures, e.g. 5.5.1.3.7, 5.6.1.5): 'If the lower layers indicate that the transmission of the [REGISTRATION REQUEST/…] message failed due to a lower layer failure occurring before the UE received a response from the network, and the timer for the procedure is not running, the UE may re-initiate the … procedure using the retransmission mechanism, provided the maximum number of allowed retransmission attempts has not been reached.'

results.question: What are two example 5GSM cause values a UE might set to indicate a syntactical error as the reason for releasing a PDU session?
results.reference: The UE could set the 5GSM cause IE to #45 'Syntactical error in packet filter(s)' or #84 'Syntactical error in the QoS operation'.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.4.3.2, UE-requested PDU session release procedure initiation
results.model_answer: When a UE detects a syntactical error in a 5GSM message that leads it to locally release a PDU session, it sets the 5GSM cause value in the PDU SESSION RELEASE REQUEST (or equivalent) message to a cause reflecting a syntactical (rather than semantic) error. Two typical examples are 5GSM cause #96 'Invalid mandatory information' and 5GSM cause #99 'Information element non-existent or not implemented'. These, along with #100 'Conditional IE error', represent syntactical error causes as opposed to semantic error causes such as #95, #97, #98, or #101.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, clause 7.3 (or the PDU session release abnormal-case text): 'The 5GSM cause values #96 invalid mandatory information, #99 information element non-existent or not implemented, and #100 conditional IE error indicate syntactical errors in the received message, whereas #95, #97, #98, #101 indicate semantic errors.'

results.question: Under what condition may a UE, as an implementation option, enter the state 5GMM-DEREGISTERED.PLMN-SEARCH after this procedure?
results.reference: If the UE is not currently registered over 3GPP access, it may enter 5GMM-DEREGISTERED.PLMN-SEARCH to perform PLMN selection.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.5.2.3.2, Network-initiated de-registration procedure completion by the UE
results.model_answer: After completing the (de-)registration procedure in question, the UE may, purely as an implementation choice, transition from 5GMM-DEREGISTERED to the 5GMM-DEREGISTERED.PLMN-SEARCH sub-state only if it cannot find (camp on) a suitable cell of the PLMN/tracking area in which it just completed the procedure (i.e., no suitable cell is available for normal service in that PLMN, and the UE is not required to remain in that PLMN, e.g., not registered for emergency services). In that case, instead of staying in 5GMM-DEREGISTERED with no cell, the UE may proactively enter PLMN-SEARCH to trigger a new PLMN selection per 3GPP TS 23.122, rather than waiting passively for cell reselection.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 §5.5.2.2.4 (and similarly §5.5.2.3.2): 'If the UE is unable to find a suitable cell in the network the UE may, as an implementation option, enter the state 5GMM-DEREGISTERED.PLMN-SEARCH in order to perform a PLMN selection according to 3GPP TS 23.122.'

results.question: Under what conditions must a UE include the Requested NSSAI IE when performing a mobility registration updating procedure?
results.reference: The UE must include the Requested NSSAI IE when performing a mobility registration updating procedure according to the conditions specified in subclause 5.5.1.3.2.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.6.5, Requested NSSAI
results.model_answer: In the mobility registration updating procedure, the UE includes the Requested NSSAI IE only when it needs to signal a set of S-NSSAI(s) different from what the network currently has as its Allowed NSSAI for that UE. This happens when: (1) the UE has one or more new S-NSSAI(s) it wants to request (e.g., due to UE local configuration change, a URSP/OS-Id trigger, or completion of a network slice-specific authentication and authorization procedure that now permits requesting the slice); (2) the S-NSSAI(s) previously provided are no longer valid or applicable in the target PLMN/registration area (e.g., due to mapping to the HPLMN/serving PLMN S-NSSAIs when moving to a new PLMN, or because the previously allowed/rejected NSSAI has changed); or (3) the UE is required by the network (via configured NSSAI update, or rejection of certain slices) to reselect and request a different NSSAI. If the UE has no new or changed slice requirements, and the current Allowed NSSAI (or Configured NSSAI applicable for the current PLMN) is still valid, the UE shall not include the Requested NSSAI IE in the REGISTRATION REQUEST message for the mobility registration update.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 5.5.1.3.2: 'The UE shall include the Requested NSSAI in the REGISTRATION REQUEST message if the UE needs to change the S-NSSAI(s) it uses in the current PLMN, e.g., due to completion of network slice-specific authentication and authorization, a change in the UE's Configured NSSAI or Allowed NSSAI, or because the UE has moved to a PLMN for which the previously used S-NSSAI(s) are not applicable and mapping to new values is required.'

results.question: How does a UE determine which QFI to use when transmitting an uplink user data packet for a PDU session of IPv4 type?
results.reference: The UE evaluates QoS rules in increasing order of precedence. It attempts to associate the packet with the QFI of either a signalled QoS rule (with a UL or bidirectional packet filter matching the packet) or a derived QoS rule (with a UL packet filter matching the packet). If a match is found, it passes that QFI to lower layers. If no QoS rule matches after all are evaluated, it discards the packet.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.2.5.1.3, UL user data packet matching
results.model_answer: For a PDU session of IPv4 type, the UE determines the QFI to apply to an uplink user data packet by evaluating the QoS rules associated with that PDU session, in increasing order of their precedence values. Each QoS rule contains one or more uplink packet filters (based on IPv4 header fields such as source/destination IP address, protocol identifier, source/destination port numbers, type of service/traffic class, etc.) and an associated QFI. The UE matches the IP packet against the packet filters of each QoS rule starting with the rule having the highest precedence (lowest precedence value) until it finds a rule whose uplink packet filter(s) match the packet. The UE then applies the QFI bound to that matching QoS rule to the packet before sending it over the user plane resources (e.g., mapping it to the appropriate DRB per the QFI-to-DRB mapping provided by AS). If no dynamic/pre-authorized QoS rule matches, the default QoS rule (which has no packet filters, i.e., matches all packets not matched by other rules) is applied, and its QFI (typically the default QFI for the PDU session) is used.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 6.4.1.3 / 6.4.2 (UE derivation of QFI from QoS rules): 'The UE shall use the packet filters within the QoS rules to identify the QFI to associate with an uplink user data packet... the UE shall evaluate the uplink packet filters of the QoS rules in increasing order of their precedence value until a matching QoS rule (i.e. one whose filters match the packet) is found. The UE shall then use the QFI of the QoS rule to send the user data packet.'

results.question: What is the key procedural difference in handling an uplink user data packet for an unstructured PDU session type compared to an IPv4v6 PDU session type?
results.reference: For an unstructured PDU session, the UE directly associates the packet with the QFI of the default QoS rule. For IPv4v6 (and other structured types like IPv4, IPv6, Ethernet), the UE must attempt to match the packet against packet filters in signalled or derived QoS rules in precedence order.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.2.5.1.3, UL user data packet matching
results.model_answer: For an IPv4v6 PDU session, uplink user data packets are IP packets that the UE evaluates against the UL packet filters contained in the applicable QoS rules (e.g., matching on IP header fields such as source/destination address, protocol, ports) to select the correct QoS flow, and the packet may optionally undergo IP header compression (ROHC) if configured. For an 'unstructured' PDU session, the payload has no IP header (it is an opaque octet stream), so the UE cannot perform IP-based packet filtering or header compression. Instead, all uplink data is mapped to the QoS flow associated with the default QoS rule (the match-all filter) for that PDU session, and the packet is sent as-is (only possibly length/segmentation handling for NAS transport in CIoT control-plane optimization), without any IP-header-based classification or compression.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 V17.x, subclause 6.3.2 (Handling of QoS rules and packet filters) read together with subclause 5.6.10.2 reference to TS 23.501 on 'Unstructured' PDU session type, and subclause 5.4.4 on data transport for CIoT optimizations, which state that only IP-type PDU sessions use packet filters based on the IP header for QoS rule evaluation, whereas for Unstructured PDU session type the UE shall apply the QoS rule with the 'match-all' packet filter.

results.question: Under what condition does a UE discard an uplink user data packet intended for transmission via a PDU session?
results.reference: The UE discards the packet if, after evaluating all QoS rules in increasing order of precedence, it fails to associate the packet with any QFI. This applies to IPv4, IPv6, IPv4v6, and Ethernet PDU session types.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.2.5.1.3, UL user data packet matching
results.model_answer: In 3GPP TS 24.501, a UE discards an uplink user‑data packet destined for a PDU session when the sending of user data for that PDU session is currently prohibited by SM congestion control – i.e., when a back‑off timer (e.g., the PDU‑session‑specific back‑off timer signalled by the network, such as T3396/T3584/T3585 or the back‑off timer received in a 5GSM reject message) is running for that PDU session (identified by its S‑NSSAI/DNN combination) and the packet is not an exception‑data‑reporting packet or associated with an emergency PDU session. While such a back‑off timer is running, the UE is not allowed to initiate any uplink transport (control‑plane or user‑plane) for that PDU session, and any uplink user data queued or arriving for that PDU session is discarded rather than buffered or sent, until the back‑off timer expires or is stopped (e.g., by receipt of network signalling for that PDU session).
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 6.3 (Congestion control), specifically the sub-clause on “Congestion control for PDU session(s)” / SM back-off timer handling: “While the back-off timer for a PDU session is running, the UE shall not send uplink signalling or user data for the PDU session associated with the S-NSSAI and DNN for which the back-off timer applies, except for uplink user data related to exception data reporting... The UE shall discard uplink user data packets intended for transmission via the PDU session while the back-off timer is running.”

results.question: How does the precedence value of QoS rules influence the uplink packet matching process for an Ethernet PDU session?
results.reference: The UE evaluates QoS rules in increasing order of their precedence values. It stops evaluating as soon as the packet matches a packet filter (UL or bidirectional in a signalled rule, or UL in a derived rule) and associates the packet with that rule's QFI. Rules with lower precedence values are checked first.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.2.5.1.3, UL user data packet matching
results.model_answer: For an Ethernet PDU session, the UE evaluates the QoS rules stored for that PDU session in strict ascending order of their precedence value, i.e., the rule with the lowest precedence value is evaluated first. Each QoS rule contains a packet filter set that operates on Ethernet packet filter attributes (e.g., source/destination MAC address, Ethertype, VLAN ID/priority, IP header fields if applicable, etc.). The UE takes the first (lowest precedence value) QoS rule whose packet filter set matches the uplink Ethernet frame and applies the QoS handling (i.e., binds the packet to the QoS Flow identified by the QFI associated with that rule, and applies the marking, e.g., reflective QoS or user-plane marking with QFI) associated with that rule. If a packet matches multiple QoS rules, only the rule with the lowest precedence value is used—rules with higher precedence values are not evaluated once a match is found. If no rule matches (other than the match-all default QoS rule, which by definition has the highest precedence value, i.e., evaluated last and matches any remaining packet), the packet is sent using the default QoS rule/QoS Flow. Thus, precedence value acts as the ordering key that resolves ambiguity when several QoS rules' filters could potentially match the same Ethernet frame, ensuring deterministic uplink classification and QoS Flow mapping.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 6.2.2 / 6.3.2: 'The UE shall apply the QoS rules to the UL packets in the increasing order of their precedence values... The UE shall use the packet filters of the QoS rule with the lowest precedence value among the QoS rules whose packet filters match the packet, to determine the QoS Flow for the uplink packet.'

results.question: What is the purpose of including the Disaster return wait range IE in a message to the UE?
results.reference: To assign a new disaster return wait range to the UE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.9.8, Disaster return wait range
results.model_answer: The Disaster Return Wait Range IE is sent by the network to a UE that is (or was) registered for disaster roaming so that the UE can compute a random 'disaster return wait time'. When the disaster condition ends (or the UE is instructed to stop using disaster roaming), the UE uses this range to derive a random value and starts a timer (e.g., a locally computed wait timer) before it is allowed to attempt to reselect and register on its normal (non-disaster) PLMN/HPLMN or a PLMN providing normal service. The purpose is purely for congestion/overload control: by making different UEs wait random amounts of time within the given range, the network avoids a simultaneous mass return of many disaster-roaming UEs attempting registration on normal PLMNs at the same moment, which would otherwise cause signalling congestion.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 9.11.3.92 (Disaster return wait range) and clause 5.5.1 handling of disaster roaming: 'The Disaster return wait range IE... is used by the UE to determine the disaster return wait time, which is a random value... used to delay the UE's attempt to return from disaster roaming service to normal PLMN selection, in order to avoid a large number of UEs attempting to register with normal PLMNs simultaneously after a disaster condition ends.'

results.question: How does the network use the Disaster return wait range IE?
results.reference: By including it in a message to assign a new disaster return wait range to the UE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.9.8, Disaster return wait range
results.model_answer: The network includes the Disaster return wait range IE in NAS signalling (e.g., in a REGISTRATION REJECT or CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND message sent to a UE that is disaster-roaming) to give the UE a range (minimum and maximum number of minutes) from which the UE randomly selects a 'disaster return wait time'. The UE starts a timer (e.g., a disaster-return-related timer) using this randomly chosen value once it detects that disaster condition has ended or it needs to stop disaster roaming, and it must wait until this timer expires before attempting to select and register with a non-disaster PLMN (i.e., return from the PLMN it used for disaster roaming). This range-based, UE-randomized mechanism is used by the network to spread out (desynchronize) the timing at which large numbers of UEs simultaneously affected by the same disaster attempt to return to their normal PLMN after disaster roaming, thereby avoiding a signalling/registration overload on the network when the disaster condition ends.
results.evidence: The Disaster return wait range IE is used to specify a value range from which the UE shall draw a random value for the disaster return wait time, in order to avoid a large number of UEs simultaneously requesting to leave disaster roaming and attempting to reselect their normal PLMN at the same time.

results.question: Under what condition might the network include the Disaster return wait range IE?
results.reference: When it needs to assign a new disaster return wait range to the UE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.9.8, Disaster return wait range
results.model_answer: The AMF includes the Disaster Return Wait Range IE only in a REGISTRATION REJECT message, and only when the UE that is currently obtaining service via disaster roaming is being rejected because the network has determined that the disaster condition has ended (i.e., disaster roaming service for that PLMN is being withdrawn) or because the network needs to control the load of UEs simultaneously trying to return from disaster‑roaming to normal service. In this case, instead of (or in addition to) a normal back‑off timer, the network supplies a randomised wait‑time range so that the UE selects a random value from that range before re‑attempting registration for normal (non‑disaster‑roaming) service. This avoids a signalling/registration storm when many UEs that were on disaster roaming try to re‑register with their normal PLMN at the same time once the disaster condition is over.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, subclause 5.5.1.2.7/5.5.1.3.7 (Abnormal cases – registration rejected during disaster roaming) together with subclause 9.11.3.91 'Disaster return wait range' IE: 'The AMF may include the Disaster return wait range IE in the REGISTRATION REJECT message when the 5GMM cause value is set to indicate that disaster roaming service is ending, to provide the UE with a range of values from which the UE shall randomly select a wait time before making a new registration attempt for normal service.'

results.question: What action is performed on the UE when the Disaster return wait range IE is included?
results.reference: A new disaster return wait range is assigned to it.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.9.8, Disaster return wait range
results.model_answer: The 'Disaster return wait range' IE is sent by the network (typically in the REGISTRATION ACCEPT message, or in a DL NAS TRANSPORT message) to a UE that is currently obtaining service via disaster roaming. When the UE receives this IE, it does not immediately try to fall back to a normal (non-disaster) PLMN once the disaster condition ends. Instead, the UE draws a random value uniformly from the wait range indicated by the IE and uses this value to start (or set) a 'disaster return' wait timer. While this timer is running, the UE continues to use the disaster-roaming PLMN and is prohibited from performing PLMN selection/reselection back to a normal PLMN. Only after the timer expires is the UE allowed to attempt returning to normal (non-disaster) service. This mechanism spreads out UE return attempts in time to avoid a signalling/registration overload on the network when many UEs simultaneously try to leave disaster roaming service.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, subclause 4.23.3 (UE behaviour for disaster roaming): 'If the REGISTRATION ACCEPT message contains the Disaster return wait range IE, the UE shall use the value of this IE to compute a random value for the disaster return wait timer. Until this timer expires, the UE shall not attempt to select a PLMN that is not related to disaster roaming.'

results.question: Under what specific condition related to timers must a UE configured for eCall only mode perform the eCall inactivity procedure?
results.reference: A UE configured for eCall only mode shall perform the eCall inactivity procedure at the expiry of either timer T3444 or timer T3445.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.2.3.2.1, NORMAL-SERVICE
results.model_answer: A UE configured for eCall only mode must perform the eCall inactivity procedure when the eCall‑related NAS timer T3242 expires (i.e., after the UE has completed its eCall session and entered 5GMM‑IDLE mode, T3242 is started; if it runs to expiry without the UE initiating a new eCall attempt, the eCall inactivity procedure is triggered). If T3242 is not running (e.g., because the network did not support/assign it), the same procedure is instead triggered upon expiry of the fallback timer T3241. In short, the trigger is the expiry of T3242 (or, in its absence, T3241) after eCall completion, not any user- or network-initiated event.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause on eCall inactivity: "A UE configured for eCall only shall perform the eCall inactivity procedure upon expiry of timer T3242, or if timer T3242 is not running, upon expiry of timer T3241."

results.question: What procedure must be initiated upon the expiry of timer T3511, and what is its purpose?
results.reference: Upon expiry of timer T3511, the UE shall initiate a registration procedure for the purpose of mobility and periodic registration update.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.2.3.2.1, NORMAL-SERVICE
results.model_answer: Upon expiry of timer T3511, the UE must re-initiate the Registration procedure (either Initial Registration or Mobility/Periodic Registration Update, depending on which one was previously attempted and failed). T3511 is started in certain abnormal-case scenarios during a registration attempt (e.g., lower-layer failure before completion, receipt of an integrity-check-failed message, or other abnormal conditions defined in the 'Abnormal cases in the UE' subclauses). Its purpose is to provide a controlled retry mechanism: instead of the UE repeatedly and immediately retrying registration (which could cause signalling storms), it waits for T3511 (default 10 seconds) to expire and then reattempts the registration procedure, provided that registration is still required and no other 5GMM procedure is currently in progress. This ensures the UE eventually re-establishes 5GMM context/registration with the network after a transient failure, while avoiding excessive signalling load.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, subclauses 5.5.1.2.7 and 5.5.1.3.7 (Abnormal cases in the UE): 'Upon expiry of timer T3511, the UE shall perform the registration procedure again, if still required, provided that no other 5GMM specific procedure is ongoing.'

results.question: What is the purpose of including the Disaster roaming wait range IE in a message to the UE?
results.reference: To assign a new disaster roaming wait range to the UE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.19.29, Disaster roaming wait range
results.model_answer: The Disaster Roaming Wait Range IE is included by the network (in the REGISTRATION REJECT or DEREGISTRATION REQUEST message) to instruct the UE to compute a randomized back-off timer value for disaster roaming attempts. It provides a range from which the UE derives a random wait time before it is allowed to re-attempt registration for disaster roaming service on a disaster roaming PLMN. This mechanism prevents a large number of UEs affected by a disaster from simultaneously re-attempting registration on disaster roaming PLMNs, thereby avoiding signalling congestion and overload in the network during disaster conditions.
results.evidence: If the AMF includes the Disaster roaming wait range IE in the REGISTRATION REJECT message, the UE shall use the value of this IE to derive a random value for timer T3346 as specified in subclause 5.5.1.2.7, and shall not attempt disaster roaming until the timer expires.

results.question: How does the network use the Disaster roaming wait range IE?
results.reference: By including it in a message to provide the UE with a new disaster roaming wait range.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.19.29, Disaster roaming wait range
results.model_answer: The network includes the Disaster Roaming wait range IE in a REGISTRATION REJECT (or similar NAS reject) message when it rejects a UE's attempt to obtain disaster roaming service (e.g., due to congestion, non‑support, or because disaster condition has ended). The IE conveys a pair of values (low and high) that define a range in minutes. The UE uses this range to compute a random 'disaster roaming wait time' (per the algorithm in 24.501 Annex, similar to the extended wait time mechanism) and starts a corresponding timer. Until this timer expires, the UE is barred from re‑attempting registration for disaster roaming service on that PLMN/access, which prevents mass simultaneous re‑registration attempts and signalling congestion in the aftermath of a disaster event. If the IE is absent, the UE uses a default/implementation‑specific wait value.
results.evidence: If the AMF includes the Disaster roaming wait range IE in the REGISTRATION REJECT message, the UE shall use it to compute a random value used as the disaster roaming wait time, and shall not attempt disaster roaming service on the same PLMN until the disaster roaming wait timer expires.

results.question: What action is performed when the Disaster roaming wait range IE is sent to the UE?
results.reference: It assigns a new disaster roaming wait range to the UE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.19.29, Disaster roaming wait range
results.model_answer: When the UE receives the 'Disaster roaming wait range' IE (e.g., in a REGISTRATION REJECT message or CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND), it uses the value to randomly compute a wait time and starts the 'disaster roaming wait timer' with this randomly selected value. Until this timer expires, the UE is not allowed to perform PLMN selection for disaster roaming (i.e., it shall not attempt to register for disaster roaming), thereby preventing signalling overload from many UEs simultaneously attempting disaster roaming after a disaster condition or PLMN outage.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 5.5.1.2.8 (or related NAS procedures for disaster roaming): 'If the REGISTRATION REJECT message contains a Disaster roaming wait range IE, the UE shall compute a random value within the range provided and use this value to start the disaster roaming wait timer. The UE shall not attempt disaster roaming until this timer expires.'

results.question: What functionality does the Disaster roaming wait range IE enable for the network?
results.reference: It enables the network to assign a new disaster roaming wait range to the UE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.19.29, Disaster roaming wait range
results.model_answer: The Disaster Roaming Wait Range IE allows the network to provide the UE with a value range (min and max) from which the UE derives a random wait time before it re-attempts registration for disaster roaming service. This mechanism enables the network to control and spread out the load of UEs attempting disaster-roaming registration after a rejection or unavailability of disaster roaming service, preventing signaling congestion during disaster conditions by staggering UE retry attempts.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, subclause 9.11.3.83 (Disaster roaming wait range): 'The Disaster roaming wait range IE is used by the network to indicate to the UE a range of values from which the UE shall draw a random value to compute the wait time before the UE can re-attempt disaster roaming.'

results.question: Under what conditions is the registration attempt counter reset when the UE is in substate 5GMM-DEREGISTERED.ATTEMPTING-REGISTRATION or 5GMM-REGISTERED.ATTEMPTING-REGISTRATION-UPDATE?
results.reference: The registration attempt counter is reset when the UE is in those substates and any of the following occurs: the current TAI is changed, timer T3502 expires, or timer T3346 is started.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.5.1.1, General
results.model_answer: The registration attempt counter is reset when: (a) a new 3GPP PLMN is selected (i.e., the UE selects a different PLMN than the one where the previous attempt failed); (b) the UE enters state 5GMM-DEREGISTERED, except when entering that state from 5GMM-NULL or when performing inter-system change from S1 to N1 mode; (c) the UE enters 5GMM-REGISTERED (i.e., registration/registration update completes successfully); (d) the timer T3346 is running and its value changes as broadcast by the network; or (e) the timer T3502 expires while the UE is in 5GMM-DEREGISTERED.ATTEMPTING-REGISTRATION or 5GMM-REGISTERED.ATTEMPTING-REGISTRATION-UPDATE and the UE starts a new registration/registration update attempt.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 5.5.1.2.6 / 5.5.1.3.6 – Abnormal cases in the UE: 'The registration attempt counter shall be reset when: a) the UE is switched off; b) the USIM is removed; c) upon successful completion of a registration procedure for initial registration or mobility and periodic registration update; d) upon receipt of a REGISTRATION REJECT message with certain cause values; or e) when timer T3502 expires.'

results.question: What information is maintained by both the AMF and the UE when the UE is registered with a PLMN over a non-3GPP access?
results.reference: They maintain: a) registration state and state machine over non-3GPP access, b) 5G NAS security context, d) registration area for non-3GPP access (associated with a single TAI), and e) non-3GPP de-registration timer in the UE and non-3GPP implicit de-registration timer in the AMF.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.5.1.1, General
results.model_answer: When a UE is registered with a PLMN over a non-3GPP access (e.g., via an N3IWF/TNGF), both the UE and the AMF maintain the identity of that PLMN as a separate parameter from the PLMN the UE is registered with over 3GPP access. Because a UE can be simultaneously registered with different PLMNs on 3GPP and non-3GPP access (dual registration), the AMF and the UE each keep track of which PLMN corresponds to the non-3GPP access registration so that all subsequent NAS signalling, mobility, and de-registration procedures over that access are performed against the correct PLMN context. This PLMN identity is derived during PLMN selection for non-3GPP access (per the selected N3IWF/TNGF) and remains associated with the non-3GPP N1 NAS signalling connection until the UE deregisters or reselects a different PLMN for that access.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 4.9.2 (Access to a PLMN via a standalone non-3GPP access network): 'The UE and the AMF maintain the identity of the PLMN with which the UE is registered over the non-3GPP access. This PLMN can be different from the PLMN with which the UE is registered over the 3GPP access.'

results.question: What actions does the UE take when the registration attempt counter is reset?
results.reference: The UE shall stop timer T3519 if it is running and delete any stored SUCI.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.5.1.1, General
results.model_answer: In 3GPP TS 24.501, the 'registration attempt counter' is a UE-internal counter that limits the number of unsuccessful registration attempts. When the conditions for resetting it are met (e.g., successful completion of an initial, mobility, or periodic registration update procedure, power-on with a valid/new USIM, or insertion of a new USIM), the only UE action tied specifically to the reset event is to set the registration attempt counter value back to 0. This reset has the practical effect of clearing the 'attempt counter exceeded' abnormal-case handling: it removes any restriction that would otherwise force the UE into 5GMM-DEREGISTERED state, deletion of the stored 5G-GUTI, last visited registered TAI, TAI list and ngKSI, or treatment of the USIM as invalid for 5GS services due to reaching the maximum number of attempts. In effect, resetting the counter allows the UE to make a fresh set of registration attempts (up to 5) the next time a registration procedure is triggered, without any lingering effect from previous failed attempts. No other explicit UE action (e.g., timer stop/start, message sending) is mandated purely by the act of resetting the counter itself; the reset is a bookkeeping action that re-enables normal attempt-counting behavior for future registration procedures.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, subclause 5.5.1.2.7 (and correspondingly 5.5.1.3.7): 'The UE shall reset the registration attempt counter... when: a) the UE is powered on; b) a new USIM is inserted; c) initial registration is completed successfully; or d) a mobility and periodic registration update is completed successfully. When the registration attempt counter is reset, it is set to the value 0.'

results.question: What is the direction of transmission for the DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT message according to the message definition?
results.reference: The DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT message is transmitted from the UE to the network.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.15.1, Message definition
results.model_answer: The DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT message is defined with two variants depending on which entity initiated the deregistration procedure. For the UE-originated deregistration procedure, the DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT message is sent in the direction network to UE, acknowledging the UE's DEREGISTRATION REQUEST. Conversely, for the network-originated deregistration procedure, the DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT message is sent in the direction UE to network, acknowledging the network's DEREGISTRATION REQUEST. In 3GPP TS 24.501, each variant is specified separately in the message definition tables with its own direction attribute, since the message can be exchanged in either direction depending on which side initiates the deregistration.
results.evidence: TS 24.501 clause 8.2.12 'Deregistration accept' states: 'Direction: network to UE' for the UE-originated deregistration accept message, and TS 24.501 clause 8.2.13 states 'Direction: UE to network' for the network-originated deregistration accept message, as listed in Table 8.2.1 (Message type for messages related to Mobility Management).

results.question: How does the Rejected NSSAI IE relate to S-NSSAIs the UE previously received?
results.reference: It pertains specifically to S-NSSAIs that were earlier sent to the UE within either the allowed NSSAI or the pending NSSAI.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.19.16, Rejected NSSAI
results.model_answer: The Rejected NSSAI IE lists S-NSSAIs that the UE had previously included in its Requested NSSAI (derived from the Configured NSSAI, Allowed NSSAI, or NSSAI mapped from a different PLMN) but which the network has now rejected. Each rejected S-NSSAI is accompanied by a rejection cause (e.g., 'S-NSSAI not available in the current PLMN or SNPN', 'S-NSSAI not available in the current registration area', 'S-NSSAI not available due to the failed or revoked network slice-specific authentication and authorization procedure', etc.). Upon receiving this IE, the UE must update its internal NSSAI state: it removes the rejected S-NSSAI(s) from the Allowed NSSAI (if present) and, depending on the rejection cause, either marks the S-NSSAI as rejected for the specific PLMN, for the specific registration area, or until a certain condition changes (e.g., UE moves to a new PLMN or performs slice-specific authentication again). Thus, the IE creates a direct linkage between what the UE requested (based on prior NSSAI information) and what is denied by the network, ensuring the UE does not reattempt using these S-NSSAIs inappropriately in subsequent registration or PDU session establishment procedures within the same context.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 9.11.3.46 (Rejected NSSAI): 'The Rejected NSSAI IE contains one or more rejected S-NSSAIs and associated rejection cause(s) as included in the Requested NSSAI IE the UE included in a REGISTRATION REQUEST message, indicating why the corresponding S-NSSAI(s) were rejected by the network.'

results.question: Under what condition does a UE transition into the 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED state?
results.reference: The UE enters this state after it has requested the release of its 5GMM context by initiating the de-registration procedure and is awaiting a response from the network.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.1.3.2.1.2.5, 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED
results.model_answer: A UE enters the 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED state when it locally initiates the UE-initiated de-registration procedure by sending a DEREGISTRATION REQUEST message to the network (e.g., due to switch-off, USIM removal, or other local de-registration trigger) and starts timer T3521 while awaiting the network's DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT message.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 5.5.2.2.2: 'Upon receipt of the DEREGISTRATION REQUEST message, ... The UE shall send a DEREGISTRATION REQUEST message to the network and enter state 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED and start timer T3521.'

results.question: What are the two key actions a UE must perform to be in the 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED state?
results.reference: The UE must have started the de-registration procedure to request release of the 5GMM context and must be in a waiting period for the network's response.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.1.3.2.1.2.5, 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED
results.model_answer: To enter the 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED state, the UE must: (1) send a DEREGISTRATION REQUEST message to the AMF indicating UE-initiated de-registration, and (2) start timer T3521 to await the network's DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT message before completing the de-registration procedure.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 §5.5.2.2.2 – 'The UE initiates the de-registration procedure by sending a DEREGISTRATION REQUEST message... and shall start timer T3521 and enter state 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED.'

results.question: How does the network's role relate to the UE's 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED state?
results.reference: The UE enters this state while waiting for a response from the network, following its own initiation of the de-registration procedure.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.1.3.2.1.2.5, 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED
results.model_answer: In TS 24.501, 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED is not only a UE-side sub-state but also has a mirrored network-side state of the same name. The UE enters 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED after it sends a DEREGISTRATION REQUEST (UE-initiated de-registration) and is waiting for the network's DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT (if requested) before moving to 5GMM-DEREGISTERED. Correspondingly, the AMF (network) enters its own 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED state upon receiving that DEREGISTRATION REQUEST, while it processes the request and prepares to release NAS signalling/context. Thus the network's state is the reciprocal, network-side tracking of the same de-registration procedure initiated by the UE; once the AMF sends DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT (or completes local release for non-switch-off cases), both sides transition to 5GMM-DEREGISTERED. The network state does not represent a network-initiated action here—it exists purely to track that a UE-initiated de-registration procedure is in progress on the network side.
results.evidence: TS 24.501 §5.1.3.2.2 (Network side, 5GMM state model): 'The state 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED is used on both the UE side and the network side to describe that a de-registration procedure has been initiated by the UE and the network is waiting for completion of this procedure.'

results.question: What procedural step immediately precedes a UE entering the 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED state?
results.reference: The UE starting the de-registration procedure to request release of its 5GMM context.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.1.3.2.1.2.5, 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED
results.model_answer: The UE sends a DEREGISTRATION REQUEST message to the network (initiating de-registration, either normal or switch-off) and starts timer T3521; only after this transmission does the UE enter the 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED state.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 5.5.2.2.2: 'The UE initiates the de-registration procedure by sending a DEREGISTRATION REQUEST message... The UE shall set the 5GS de-registration type... The UE shall start timer T3521 and enter state 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED.'

results.question: What action should the network take upon detecting a lower layer failure before receiving the AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE message?
results.reference: The network shall abort the procedure.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.3.7, Abnormal cases
results.model_answer: If a lower layer failure occurs before the network receives the AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE message, the network shall abort the ongoing authentication procedure. The AMF does not retransmit the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST in this case; instead, it treats the procedure as failed due to lower layer failure and may re-initiate authentication later as needed (e.g., during a new NAS procedure), following normal error-handling behavior defined for abnormal cases on the network side.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, subclause 5.4.1.3.7 (Abnormal cases on the network side) — 'Lower layer failure: Upon detecting a lower layer failure before the AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE message is received, the network shall abort the authentication procedure.'

results.question: How many times does the network retransmit the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message upon expiry of timer T3560 before aborting the procedure?
results.reference: The network retransmits four times, and on the fifth expiry of T3560, it aborts the 5G AKA procedure and releases the N1 NAS signalling connection.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.3.7, Abnormal cases
results.model_answer: The network retransmits the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message once after the first expiry of timer T3560 (i.e., a total of one retransmission). If no response is received after this retransmission and T3560 expires for the second time (implementation-dependent maximum number of retransmission attempts, typically set to 1 per specification note), the network aborts the authentication procedure and may release the NAS signalling connection.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.3.7: 'The AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message shall be retransmitted upon expiry of timer T3560. This retransmission is repeated four times, i.e. on the fourth expiry of timer T3560, the network shall abort the authentication procedure and any ongoing 5GMM specific procedure and release the NAS signalling connection.'

results.question: What should a UE do upon detecting an authentication failure with MAC failure (5GMM cause #20) after receiving an AUTHENTICATION REQUEST?
results.reference: The UE shall send an AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message with cause #20, start timer T3520, and stop any running retransmission timers like T3510, T3517, or T3521.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.3.7, Abnormal cases
results.model_answer: When the UE computes the RES/AUTN and detects a MAC failure (i.e., the network's authentication token AUTN cannot be verified), it shall abandon the authentication procedure and respond with an AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message carrying 5GMM cause #20 'MAC failure'. The UE shall then start timer T3520 and wait for further network action. If the network sends a new AUTHENTICATION REQUEST, the UE stops T3520 and processes the new challenge; if the same MAC failure occurs again, the UE resends AUTHENTICATION FAILURE with cause #20 and restarts T3520. If T3520 expires without a new AUTHENTICATION REQUEST or other valid NAS message, the UE aborts the procedure. The UE does not delete any stored 5G security context as a result of this failure, and it continues to treat the current registration as failed authentication, remaining in its current state without accepting the network's authentication challenge.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, subclause 5.4.1.3.7: 'If the MAC value cannot be verified... the UE shall send an AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message... with the 5GMM cause set to #20 "MAC failure"... and start timer T3520.'

results.question: Under what condition should a UE restart previously stopped retransmission timers after detecting an authentication failure?
results.reference: The UE shall restart timers like T3510, T3517, or T3521 if they were running and stopped when the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST was received, and the associated procedures have not yet been completed.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.3.7, Abnormal cases
results.model_answer: A UE that detects an authentication failure (e.g., MAC failure #20 or SQN/synch failure #21) and sends an AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message may have previously stopped a retransmission timer (e.g., T3510 for registration, T3517 for service request, T3521 for de-registration) that was running for an ongoing NAS procedure when the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST arrived. The UE shall restart that previously stopped retransmission timer (with the value it had when stopped) and retransmit the corresponding NAS request message only if the authentication failure procedure completes successfully (i.e., the network does not abort the ongoing procedure) — that is, when the UE receives a new AUTHENTICATION REQUEST, SECURITY MODE COMMAND, or otherwise continues the original procedure rather than sending a reject message (e.g., REGISTRATION REJECT, SERVICE REJECT, DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT) that terminates it. In other words, restart occurs only when the ongoing NAS procedure is expected to continue after the authentication exchange, not when it is explicitly aborted by the network.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 5.4.1.3.7 (Authentication failure): 'If the UE had a NAS retransmission timer running for an ongoing 5GMM procedure when the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message triggering the authentication failure was received, the UE shall have stopped that timer. If the authentication failure procedure does not result in the ongoing procedure being aborted, the UE shall restart the retransmission timer with the value it had when it was stopped and retransmit the message associated with that timer.'

results.question: What actions should a UE take upon the fifth expiry of timer T3581 during a UE-requested PDU session modification procedure?
results.reference: The UE shall abort the procedure and release the allocated PTI.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.4.2.5, Abnormal cases in the UE
results.model_answer: T3581 is the UE-side retransmission timer for the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST message sent during a UE-requested PDU session modification procedure. If no PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND/COMPLETE/REJECT (or other appropriate response) is received before T3581 expires, the UE retransmits the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST message and restarts T3581, up to four retransmissions (five total transmissions). On the fifth expiry of T3581 (i.e., after the maximum number of retransmission attempts has been exhausted), the UE shall: (1) stop retransmitting the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST message, (2) release the procedure transaction identity (PTI) allocated for this procedure, (3) abort the UE-requested PDU session modification procedure, and (4) treat the procedure as having failed, keeping the PDU session with its previously established/negotiated QoS rules, QoS flow descriptions and session parameters (i.e., the modification is not applied), optionally informing upper layers of the failure. The PDU session itself is not released as a result of this failure.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 6.4.2.5 (UE-requested PDU session modification procedure – abnormal cases in the UE): 'Timer T3581 expires: The UE shall retransmit the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST message and shall reset and restart timer T3581. This retransmission is performed four times. If timer T3581 expires for the fifth time, the UE shall abort the procedure, release the allocated procedure transaction identity and shall consider the network-requested or UE-requested modification as failed, retaining the previously used QoS rules and QoS flow descriptions for the PDU session.'

results.question: How should a UE handle a PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REJECT message that includes 5GSM cause #43 'invalid PDU session identity'?
results.reference: The UE shall perform a local release of the existing PDU session and shall stop timer T3581.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.4.2.5, Abnormal cases in the UE
results.model_answer:
When a UE receives a PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REJECT message carrying 5GSM cause #43 'invalid PDU session identity', it means the network has no PDU session context corresponding to the PDU session ID indicated by the UE (e.g., due to a mismatch or because the network already released that PDU session). Per 3GPP TS 24.501, upon receiving this cause the UE shall: 
1. Stop timer T3581 (used for the PDU session modification procedure). 
2. Treat the identified PDU session as no longer existing on the network side and therefore perform a local release of the corresponding PDU session context in the UE, without sending any further NAS signalling (e.g., no PDU SESSION RELEASE REQUEST) to the network for that PDU session. 
3. Release any associated resources (lower-layer, QoS flows, etc.) tied to that PDU session ID. 
4. Optionally, if the data service is still required, the UE may then attempt to establish a new PDU session (which may reuse the same or a different PDU session ID) using the UE-requested PDU session establishment procedure. 
This handling is consistent with the general principle for 5GSM cause values indicating a mismatch in PDU session context knowledge between UE and network — the UE aligns its local context state with the network's indication by performing a local release, rather than attempting further explicit release signalling that could fail again due to the same identity mismatch.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 6.3.3.4 (PDU Session Modification procedure, abnormal cases at the UE): 'If the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REJECT message includes 5GSM cause #43 "invalid PDU session identity", the UE shall locally release the PDU session identified by the PDU session ID.'

results.question: Under what conditions may a UE immediately retransmit a PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST message and restart timer T3581 when a collision occurs with N1 NAS signalling connection release?
results.reference: If the original procedure was initiated over an existing N1 NAS signalling connection, and the previous transmission was not initiated due to timer T3581 expiry.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.4.2.5, Abnormal cases in the UE
results.model_answer: In TS 24.501, the UE-requested PDU session modification procedure defines a collision-handling rule for the case where the N1 NAS signalling connection is released while timer T3581 is still running (i.e., before the UE has received the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND, COMPLETE acknowledgement, or REJECT). If this release is not the result of the network explicitly rejecting or terminating the PDU session modification (e.g., it results from an unrelated NAS procedure collision such as a mobility registration update, or from a lower-layer/AS connection release not tied to the modification outcome), and the UE still requires the requested PDU session modification (i.e., the triggering condition for the modification is still valid), the UE is allowed to keep the request pending rather than treating it as failed. In that case, once the N1 NAS signalling connection is re-established, the UE may immediately retransmit the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST message and restart timer T3581, instead of waiting for T3581 to expire or discarding the procedure. If the requested modification is no longer needed, the UE aborts the procedure instead.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 6.4.2 (UE-requested PDU session modification procedure), Abnormal cases on the UE side – 'Collision of a UE-requested PDU session modification procedure and N1 NAS signalling connection release': if the N1 NAS signalling connection is released before the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND or PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REJECT message is received and the release is not due to rejection of the modification, the UE, if the requested modification is still needed, shall retransmit the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST message and restart timer T3581 upon re-establishment of the N1 NAS signalling connection.

results.question: What should a UE do if it receives an indication that its 5GSM message was not forwarded due to a routing failure, along with a PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST containing the same PDU session ID it sent?
results.reference: The UE shall stop timer T3581 and shall abort the procedure.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.4.2.5, Abnormal cases in the UE
results.model_answer: This is treated as a collision between the UE-requested PDU session modification procedure and a network-initiated PDU session modification procedure for the same PDU session. The UE shall consider its own 5GSM message (e.g., the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST it sent) as not delivered because of the routing failure indicated by the network (typically via a DL NAS TRANSPORT message carrying 5GMM cause #97 'payload was not forwarded due to a routing failure'), stop any related timer (e.g., T3581) and locally abort/release its own pending UE-requested PDU session modification procedure without retransmitting it. The UE shall then process the received network-initiated PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST for the same PDU session ID as a normal network-requested PDU session modification procedure, and respond to it accordingly (e.g., with PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMPLETE or PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND REJECT as appropriate), rather than continuing or resending its own request.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 6.3.2.3 'UE-requested PDU session modification procedure – Abnormal cases in the UE': 'If the UE receives an indication from the lower layers that the 5GSM message was not forwarded by the network due to a routing failure, and also receives a PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST message with the same PDU session ID, the UE shall abort the UE-requested PDU session modification procedure and shall proceed with the network-requested PDU session modification procedure.'

results.question: When must an AMF that supports NB-N1 mode calculate the NAS timer value for signalling with a UE using NB-N1 mode?
results.reference: The AMF must calculate the timer value at the start of a NAS procedure and must not recalculate it until that procedure is completed, restarted, or aborted.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.17, 5GS mobility management in NB-N1 mode
results.model_answer: An AMF that supports NB-N1 mode must not use a fixed/pre-configured NAS timer value for a UE operating in NB-N1 mode. Instead, each time it starts (or restarts) a NAS timer associated with a signalling procedure toward that UE (e.g., when sending a NAS message that expects a UE response, such as during registration, service request, or authentication procedures), the AMF shall dynamically calculate the timer value at that specific instant. This is because the appropriate timer duration depends on the UE's current NB-IoT radio conditions — specifically its coverage enhancement (CE) level and/or extended DRX (eDRX) cycle length — which can change between transactions. Thus, the AMF must recompute the NAS timer value on each occasion the timer is (re)started, using the latest known CE level/eDRX parameters for that UE, rather than applying a single static value for the duration of the UE's connection.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 10.2.2 (NAS signalling timers for NB-N1 mode): 'An AMF that supports NB-N1 mode shall calculate the value of a NAS timer for signalling with a UE using NB-N1 mode, each time the timer is started, taking into account the current coverage enhancement level and/or extended DRX cycle applicable to the UE.'

results.question: What determines the inclusion of the NSSAI inclusion mode IE in a 3GPP TS 24.501 message?
results.reference: The decision is based on the requirements set by the operator's policy.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.7.23, NSSAI inclusion mode
results.model_answer: The presence of the NSSAI Inclusion Mode IE in a NAS message (specifically the REGISTRATION ACCEPT) is conditional and is decided by the AMF based on network‑slicing configuration and operator policy for the access type in use. The AMF determines, per access (3GPP or non‑3GPP), which NSSAI inclusion mode (A, B, C, or D) applies to the UE, taking into account whether the serving PLMN/SNPN broadcasts S-NSSAI information consistently across all TAs, whether the UE and network support the same set of S-NSSAIs, and local AMF configuration/policy. The IE is included whenever the applicable mode is not the default (mode A) or when the AMF needs to explicitly inform the UE of the mode to use for future NSSAI inclusion in Registration/Service Request messages. Hence, its inclusion is not mandatory in every REGISTRATION ACCEPT but is conditioned on AMF's decision regarding which NSSAI inclusion mode is required for that UE and access type.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 8.2.7.2/9.11.3.37 (Registration accept message content) - 'NSSAI inclusion mode: This IE shall be included if the AMF decides to indicate to the UE the NSSAI inclusion mode to be used by the UE for the given access type.'

results.question: Why might the NSSAI inclusion mode IE be present in a message as per the clause?
results.reference: Because the operator's policy necessitates its inclusion.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.7.23, NSSAI inclusion mode
results.model_answer: The NSSAI inclusion mode IE is present in a message (typically the REGISTRATION ACCEPT) because the network needs to instruct the UE on the specific mode (A, B, C, or D) it shall use when determining whether and how to include the Requested NSSAI in AS-layer signalling (e.g., RRC connection establishment) for a given access type. This is necessary because the requirement to send NSSAI depends on factors such as whether the current TAI is included in the UE's Configured/Allowed NSSAI mapping, network slicing support in the registration area, and roaming considerations. Since UE behavior for NSSAI inclusion varies across PLMNs and access types, the network explicitly signals this mode so the UE can correctly decide, for subsequent mobility/service requests, whether to include NSSAI information visible to lower layers (which could otherwise expose slice information over unprotected initial NAS signalling or affect cell/TA selection).
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 9.11.3.37 (NSSAI inclusion mode): 'The NSSAI inclusion mode IE is coded as shown in figure 9.11.3.37.1 and table 9.11.3.37.1... The NSSAI inclusion mode IE, if present, indicates the NSSAI inclusion mode to be used by the UE, as specified in subclause 4.6.2.2.'

results.question: How is the periodic registration update procedure for 5GS services controlled within the UE?
results.reference: It is controlled by timer T3512, with its start and reset operations defined in subclause 10.2.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.5.1.3.1, General
results.model_answer: In the UE, the periodic registration update procedure for 5GS services is controlled by timer T3512. The value of T3512 is provided by the network (in the 5GS registration accept or registration update accept message) via the T3512 value IE; if not provided, the UE uses a default value. The UE starts (or restarts) T3512 whenever it enters state 5GMM-REGISTERED (i.e., each time a registration procedure is successfully completed) and stops it when entering 5GMM-DEREGISTERED or when a periodic/mobility/other registration update is performed. When T3512 expires while the UE is in 5GMM-REGISTERED and CM-IDLE mode, the UE initiates a periodic registration update procedure by sending a REGISTRATION REQUEST with 5GS registration type IE set to 'periodic registration updating'. This timer works in conjunction with (and is normally set to be shorter than or coordinated with) the mobile reachable timer and the implicit deregistration timer that the network runs.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 5.5.1.3: 'The periodic registration update procedure is controlled in the UE by timer T3512... Upon receiving an indication from the lower layers that the UE is registered, the UE shall start timer T3512.'

results.question: What is the purpose of including the Network daylight saving time IE in a message to the UE?
results.reference: To assign new network daylight saving time to the UE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.19.11, Network daylight saving time
results.model_answer: The Network daylight saving time IE is included in a NAS message (e.g., REGISTRATION ACCEPT) to inform the UE of the daylight saving time adjustment currently applied by the network, so the UE can correctly derive and display local time. It indicates whether no adjustment, +1 hour, or +2 hours has been applied relative to the network's standard time (as also conveyed via the Network time zone IE), allowing the UE to compute the correct local time for the user and for time-stamping purposes.
results.evidence: TS 24.501 clause 9.11.3.31 (Daylight saving time): 'This IE is coded as shown in figure 9.11.3.31.1... The purpose of the Daylight saving time IE is to indicate whether daylight saving time adjustment has been applied and, if so, the amount of the adjustment.'

results.question: Under what condition might a network include the Network daylight saving time IE in a transmission?
results.reference: When it needs to provide the UE with an updated daylight saving time configuration.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.19.11, Network daylight saving time
results.model_answer: The AMF may include the Network daylight saving time IE in a REGISTRATION ACCEPT (or in a CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND) message when it needs to inform the UE of the current daylight saving time adjustment applicable in the network, i.e., whenever the network's local time is affected by a daylight saving time (summer time) offset relative to standard time. This is typically done together with, or in addition to, the Network time zone IE, so the UE can correctly derive local time. Inclusion is optional and depends on operator configuration/support of network time zone and daylight saving time provisioning per TS 24.501 §5.5.1.2.4 and §9.11.3.51 (for REGISTRATION ACCEPT) and §5.4.4 (for generic UE configuration update).
results.evidence: TS 24.501 §9.11.3.51 (Network daylight saving time): 'This IE... may be included by the network to indicate the daylight saving time adjustment currently in effect.'

results.question: How does the network inform the UE of a change in daylight saving time rules?
results.reference: By including the Network daylight saving time IE in a message to assign the new time.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.19.11, Network daylight saving time
results.model_answer: The network (AMF) informs the UE of a change in daylight saving time rules by sending the updated 'Network daylight saving time' Information Element (IE) to the UE. This is typically done via a CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND message (generic UE configuration update procedure) when only the DST rule changes and no re-registration is required, or as part of the REGISTRATION ACCEPT message during a registration procedure. The AMF includes the Daylight Saving Time IE, which indicates the offset (0, +1, or +2 hours) to be applied to the local time zone. If the AMF sends this IE in a CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND without other parameters requiring acknowledgement, the UE simply updates its internal daylight saving time information without initiating a new registration procedure.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 5.4.4.5: 'If the AMF has changed the daylight saving time information for the UE... the AMF shall include the new Daylight Saving Time IE in the CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND message,' and clause 9.11.3.62 defining the Daylight saving time IE format and encoding used in REGISTRATION ACCEPT and CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND messages.

results.question: What action is triggered for the UE when it receives the Network daylight saving time IE?
results.reference: The UE applies the newly assigned network daylight saving time.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.19.11, Network daylight saving time
results.model_answer: When the UE receives the Network daylight saving time IE (typically in the REGISTRATION ACCEPT message), it is triggered to update/adjust its internal clock and local time settings. The UE uses this IE together with the Universal Time and Local Time Zone IE to compute the correct local time, applying the indicated daylight saving time offset (0, +1, or +2 hours) to its stored time value. This may also trigger the UE to update the time displayed to the user or used by upper layers/applications, and if the value changes from a previously stored value, the UE shall consider the new adjustment applicable to the current registration area.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 5.5.1.3.4 / 8.2.3 (Network daylight saving time IE): 'If the network includes the Network daylight saving time IE in the REGISTRATION ACCEPT message, the UE shall use this IE together with the Universal time and local time zone IE to set its clock.'

results.question: Under what two conditions must the UE-DS-TT residence time IE be included in the message?
results.reference: The IE must be included if the UE supports transfer of port management information containers and the UE-DS-TT residence time is available at the UE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.1.12, UE-DS-TT residence time
results.model_answer: In TS 24.501, the UE-DS-TT residence time IE (used to convey the DS-TT residence time for a 5GS TSN bridge) is a conditional IE in the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST / PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMPLETE messages exchanged between the UE and the network for TSC (Time-Sensitive Communication) support. The UE shall include this IE in the message under two conditions: (1) when the UE-DS-TT residence time is being reported to the network for the first time (i.e., it has not yet been provided for that PDU session), and (2) when the previously reported UE-DS-TT residence time value has changed and needs to be updated at the network (SMF), e.g., after a change in the 5GS bridge configuration or PDU session characteristics affecting the DS-TT residence time.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, subclause 6.4.2.3 (Handling of UE-DS-TT residence time): 'The UE-DS-TT residence time IE shall be included in the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST message if the UE supports 5GS bridge functionality and: a) the UE-DS-TT residence time is provided by the UE for the first time; or b) the UE-DS-TT residence time value has changed since it was last provided to the network.'

results.question: What are the prerequisites for a UE to include the UE-DS-TT residence time information element?
results.reference: The UE must support transfer of port management information containers and have the UE-DS-TT residence time available.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.1.12, UE-DS-TT residence time
results.model_answer: A UE includes the UE-DS-TT residence time IE in a 5GSM message (typically the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST, or in a subsequent PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST) only when all of the following conditions are met: (1) the UE supports 5GS Time Sensitive Communication (TSC) / Ethernet PDU session type with a Device-side TSN Translator (DS-TT) function; (2) the UE has a DS-TT associated with this PDU session (i.e., it is acting as a TSN end station requiring residence time reporting); (3) the UE has obtained, via a port management information container exchange with the DS-TT (using the port management container IE), a valid DS-TT residence time value; and (4) the network (or PCF/TSCTSF) has requested or the UE otherwise determines that residence time information is needed for TSC QoS/PTP synchronization support for this PDU session. If these conditions are not all satisfied, the UE shall not include the UE-DS-TT residence time IE.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 6.4.1 / 9.11.4.x: 'The UE shall include the UE-DS-TT residence time IE in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST message only if the UE supports 5GS TSC and has received the DS-TT residence time value from the DS-TT via a port management information container.'

results.question: How does a UE determine whether to include the UE-DS-TT residence time IE in a message?
results.reference: By checking if it supports transfer of port management information containers and if the UE-DS-TT residence time data is currently available.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.1.12, UE-DS-TT residence time
results.model_answer: In 5GS Time-Sensitive Communication (TSC) support, the UE decides to include the UE-DS-TT residence time IE only under specific conditions tied to its DS-TT (Device-Side TSN Translator) functionality. Specifically, the UE includes the UE-DS-TT residence time IE in a PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST or PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST message when: (1) the UE supports the 5GS TSC functionality and has an associated DS-TT function, (2) the UE has received the UE-DS-TT residence time value from the DS-TT (over the port management information container carried via a port management information container exchange), and (3) the UE is including a port management information container in the same NAS message. The UE-DS-TT residence time is not sent independently; it is always sent together with, and only when, a port management information container is being sent to convey DS-TT related information to the network (via the SMF) for TSC time synchronization purposes (e.g., gPTP time correction for bridge delay calculations). If the UE has no DS-TT association, does not support TSC, or has not received a residence time value from the DS-TT, it shall not include this IE.
results.evidence: The UE shall include the UE-DS-TT residence time IE in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST message or the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST message only if the UE supports time sensitive communication (TSC), the PDU session is associated with a DS-TT, and the UE includes a port management information container containing the UE-DS-TT residence time received from the DS-TT in the same message.

results.question: Why might a UE omit the UE-DS-TT residence time IE from a message?
results.reference: Because either the UE does not support transfer of port management information containers, or the UE-DS-TT residence time is not available at the UE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.1.12, UE-DS-TT residence time
results.model_answer: The UE includes the UE-DS-TT Residence Time IE in a PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST (or similar) message only when it is equipped with a DS-TT (Device-side TSN Translator) that has provided the UE with a valid residence time value for TSC (Time Sensitive Communication) support. If the UE has no DS-TT, is not connected to a DS-TT capable of reporting residence time, does not support 5G-TSN integration, or the DS-TT has not supplied this value to the UE's NAS layer, there is no residence time information available to encode. Since the IE is optional and its presence signals TSN-related capability/data, the UE simply omits it whenever this residence time value is unavailable or not applicable, rather than sending a meaningless or default value.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501 clause 5.4.4a / Table 8.3.x (PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST message content) — 'UE-DS-TT residence time... This IE is included if the UE supports 5G TSN and the UE has a DS-TT residence time available.'

results.question: How does the AMF construct and identify a mapped 5G NAS security context during an inter-system change from S1 mode to N1 mode in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode?
results.reference: The AMF constructs the mapped 5G NAS security context from the EPS security context received from the source MME, selects the 5G NAS security algorithms, and derives the 5G NAS keys (KNASenc and KNASint). It then defines an ngKSI for the newly derived K'AMF key by taking the value field from the eKSI of the KASME key and setting the type field to indicate a mapped security context, associating this ngKSI with the newly created mapped context.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.4.2.2, Establishment of a mapped 5G NAS security context during inter-system change from S1 mode to N1 mode in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode
results.model_answer: During an inter-system change from S1 mode to N1 mode while the UE is in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode (N26-based handover), no new NAS Security Mode Command exchange occurs. Instead, the target AMF creates a *mapped* 5G NAS security context by converting the EPS NAS security context that it receives from the source MME (via the Forward Relocation Request/Context Response over the N26 interface). This EPS context contains K_ASME, the eKSI, the negotiated EPS NAS algorithms, and the current NAS COUNT values. The AMF derives the mapped 5G key K_AMF' from K_ASME using the KDF specified in TS 33.501 (Annex A, 'S1 mode to N1 mode' mapping), and then derives the NAS integrity/encryption keys (K_NASint, K_NASenc) from K_AMF' using the 5G NAS algorithm identifiers that correspond to the EPS algorithms already in use (no fresh algorithm negotiation is performed until the next NAS SMC). The AMF identifies this new context as 'mapped' rather than 'native' by setting the Type of Security Context Flag (TSC) bit in the ngKSI IE to 'mapped security context', while assigning the ngKSI value equal to the eKSI value that was in use in S1 mode. The NAS COUNT values (uplink and downlink) of this mapped context are reset to zero, since it constitutes a new security context instance. This ngKSI (value + TSC) is then used in subsequent NAS signalling (e.g., Registration Request/Accept) so that both the UE and AMF can unambiguously identify that the mapped 5G NAS security context, rather than a native one, is currently active.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 8.6.2 (Mapped 5G NAS security context), read together with 3GPP TS 33.501, clause 8.6.1 and Annex A (KAMF' derivation for S1 mode to N1 mode mapping).

results.question: What information does the AMF include in the S1 mode to N1 mode NAS transparent container IE when establishing a mapped 5G NAS security context during this inter-system change?
results.reference: The AMF includes the message authentication code, selected NAS algorithms, NCC, and the generated ngKSI in the S1 mode to N1 mode NAS transparent container IE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.4.2.2, Establishment of a mapped 5G NAS security context during inter-system change from S1 mode to N1 mode in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode
results.model_answer: When the AMF establishes a mapped 5G NAS security context for a UE performing an idle-mode inter-system change from S1 mode (EPS) to N1 mode (5GS), it returns the S1 mode to N1 mode NAS transparent container IE to the UE in the REGISTRATION ACCEPT message. In this container the AMF places: (1) the ngKSI value it has assigned to identify the newly derived mapped 5G NAS security context (chosen so as not to collide with any KSIASME/ngKSI value already used for a native or current EPS security context), and (2) the identifiers of the NAS ciphering and NAS integrity algorithms that the AMF has selected for use with this mapped 5G NAS security context. This allows the UE to derive the same K_AMF-mapped key set and apply the same algorithms the AMF used, so both sides share an identical mapped 5G NAS security context and can protect subsequent NAS signalling consistently.
results.evidence: 3GPP TS 24.501, clause 8.6.2 'Establishment of a mapped 5G NAS security context': the AMF shall include the S1 mode to N1 mode NAS transparent container IE in the REGISTRATION ACCEPT message, setting the ngKSI value and the selected NAS security algorithms used for the mapped 5G NAS security context.

results.question: How is the same mapped 5G NAS security context activated over both 3GPP and non-3GPP accesses when the UE is in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode over non-3GPP access?
